description:
For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.
Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years.
He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school.
Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.
Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random.
text:
Gerson Turcios didn’t recognise the men standing next to a couple of dark SUVs outside his house one July afternoon last year. He figured they were lost and approached to see if he could help. A slim 23-year-old with short dark hair and big brown eyes, Turcios had just finished work mowing lawns in the pretty town of Rhinebeck, in New York’s Hudson Valley. The men asked if he knew someone called Jimmy – he did, but Jimmy hadn’t lived in the small, white weatherboard house with Turcios, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend for a while.

The men noted Turcios’s accent and asked where he was from. Turcios didn’t answer, so one took out his phone and snapped a photograph. The next thing Turcios knew, he was in handcuffs in the back of one of the SUVs and on his way to an ICE processing centre in Newburgh, New York, then on to a detention centre.

Mass deportation has been the defining mission of Donald Trump’s second presidency. In the year since he took office, ICE – United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement – has deported nearly a quarter of a million people from inside the US (half a million including from its borders) as part of an immigration crackdown. These forceful apprehensions, which have in some cases resulted in fatal shootings of potential deportees and bystanders, have resulted in protests – and sparked international outrage. Behind the statistics, though, are stories of hope and perseverance; of young immigrants who risked everything crossing rivers and deserts to build lives, start businesses and put down roots in communities that are now fighting to keep them.

Back then, as he was shackled and led to his cell, sure he was about to be deported back to Honduras, Turcios – an immigrant who had made a terrifying journey as a teenager, fleeing violence there – had no idea that his community in Rhinebeck was already mobilising; that they would raise tens of thousands of dollars in days, galvanise support from Hollywood actors and film-makers who also called the town home, and even recruit the lawyer who essentially wrote the book on stopping ICE deportations around the nation to represent him.

I’d moved to Rhinebeck with my own family from Texas during the pandemic, drawn to the bucolic countryside and good schools. Our own daughter now walks the same high school hallways Turcios once did. For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.

“Well, it’s happened,” wrote actor Griffin Dunne on Instagram. “ICE has come to my beloved Dutchess County and kidnapped a hard working kid with his own local lawn care business, and without a criminal record, off our tranquil streets.” But he added, “This is only the beginning.” Dunne, who has a home in Rhinebeck, told his followers that the community had started a war chest to defend Turcios. “Our pressure has brought about a hearing for Gerson at 11:00 tomorrow morning at Thurgood Marshall Courthouse for those who wish to show support. To my Rhinebeck neighbors, a bus will leave from Tops [grocery store] at 7:00 am.”

Six years earlier, around 9pm on a freezing December night, Turcios and three other migrants had stood by the southern banks of the Rio Grande river in Mexico, looking across into Texas as flames torched the desert brush behind them; Mexican soldiers had set it alight to flush them out.

With nowhere left to go, Turcios turned to the others. “We are right here,” he told them. “The other side is the United States.” Another boy checked that everyone was able to swim – they were – but all Gerson could think about was alligators, which had occasionally been known to inhabit the Rio Grande.

The four boys jumped into the black water together, fighting the current as it pushed them downstream. Along that stretch, near McAllen, Texas, the width of the Rio Grande ranges from 45 to 90 meters. Finally, soaking wet, they scrambled up a concrete wall on the US side. They ran through scrubland until headlights appeared behind them, then three German shepherds. A heavier boy was dragged down by the dogs as he scaled a fence; the others scattered. Turcios sprinted until three cars boxed him in and US immigration officers emerged with guns drawn. “If you keep running,” they shouted, “we’re gonna shoot your legs.” Turcios stopped, put his hands up, then fell to his knees and felt a boot between his shoulder blades as they threw him to the ground and handcuffed him. He had spent six weeks on a journey that had nearly broken him. Against all odds, he had made it across the river. And now he’d been caught.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, an adult detained by Border Patrol crossing into the US was increasingly likely to be sent back to Mexico to wait for their immigration case to be heard. Turcios, though, was under 18, and the law dictated he be taken to refugee resettlement housing for minors. Turcios stayed at a facility in Long Island for almost a month until his brother, Henoch, and Henoch’s girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, were allowed to pick him up and return to Weigel’s home in Rhinebeck.

Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years. Their first stop was a Wendy’s fast food joint for a burger – “So big,” Turcios now recalls, “I didn’t know how to eat it.”

He would have to wait for the government to notify him of his first immigration hearing, but soon the Covid pandemic would throw the courts into chaos, with some hearings postponed indefinitely and others rescheduled then postponed again, leaving Turcios in limbo.

Weigel showed Turcios his room, then drove him across the river to a big outlet store in the city of Kingston to buy clothes. He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school. In the summer of 2020, ahead of the start of the school year, he was introduced to Anna Lawson, who would be one of his classmates. Lawson was in advanced Spanish and, as Covid was still forcing people to meet virtually, they spoke regularly over Zoom. “He is a really lovely, positive person,” Lawson says. “He’d often be sitting outside, talking about how much he enjoyed Rhinebeck.”

On the first day of school, Turcios was afraid he’d be arrested by the police officer who sat outside in his car for an hour each morning as kids entered the building – just under half of US state schools have police patrol on campus – but after his first day, that fear passed. “After that I wasn’t afraid. I was excited,” he says. “But I didn’t speak any English at all.” Turcios immediately hit it off with his classmates. Brendan Dougherty shared a study hall with him. “Gerson is a very sociable guy, so it wasn’t difficult to strike up a conversation with him,” Dougherty says. “And his English progressed very quickly. Each day we’d go outside and play basketball.”

Turcios finished high school in the early summer of 2022 and began working in the kitchen of a local French restaurant and, in his spare time, for a crew that did landscaping and house maintenance, and mowed lawns. One of his first clients was Jenny Friedberg, a creative director and producer who had moved up to Rhinebeck from the city during the pandemic. Turcios and the maintenance crew painted her basement in Brooklyn, and excavated 24in of bedrock under her barn in Rhinebeck. “Whatever they did, Gerson was always there,” Friedberg says. “He was the youngest of the crew, the smiliest, the most helpful, and my favourite.”

In the summer of 2025, Turcios left the restaurant and went to work full-time with the crew. At 7.30pm on 18 July 2025, Friedberg’s phone rang. It was Carlos, Turcios’s boss. Turcios had been detained by ICE, he told her, and he didn’t know what to do.

Friedberg made several calls that evening. The first was to Luciano Valdivia, a local restaurateur and president of Rhinebeck’s chamber of commerce. The next was to Amanda Miller, a local attorney. Then John Reinish, a political communications strategist she knew. Within 24 hours, they’d set up a Spotfund, an online fundraising platform, to raise money for Turcios’s legal battle. Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.

Copeland was a nationally recognised civil rights and immigration attorney, and co-founder of the Rapid Defense Network, a non-profit providing pro bono legal support to immigrants facing deportation. He was also the subject of the documentary Guerrilla Habeas, which looked at the legal strategy it employed to stop deportations at the last moment. That strategy hinged on filing habeas corpus petitions, which empower federal judges to compel the authorities to justify detentions, a power enshrined in the constitution. Doing this forces cases out of immigration courts and into federal court, where due process can be properly considered and immigrants have a fairer shot at justice.

Miller says Copeland had experience fighting “the biggest machine there is – the federal government”. But since his move to Rhinebeck, he had stopped practising civil rights and immigration law, and had turned his attention to estate planning for clients. Still, Miller knew there was no one better to help Turcios.

“It wasn’t clear to me immediately that I would help him, but I went into triage mode, gathering information and figuring out what our options were,” Copeland says. As soon as Copeland got Turcios’s “A-Number” – the alien registration number assigned by the US Department of Homeland Security to non-citizens– he could check his status in the system. He discovered that, years earlier, Turcios had been ordered deported “in absentia” for missing a hearing. During Covid, courts repeatedly moved locations; Turcios missed a notice despite living at the same address he’d always provided.

Copeland knew it was now vital to get the Rhinebeck community to show up for him. “If you consider what the government evaluates when justifying someone’s detention, it’s whether they’re a danger to the community and a flight risk,” Copeland says. “The community is typically not going to show up for a dangerous person. And you’re less of a flight risk if there’s a strong community around you.”

It was a matter of urgency to identify where Turcios was being taken and where he was going next. Copeland says it’s not an exact science, but after working these cases as long as he had, you get a feel for it. A red flag was if he had been sent to Louisiana, a staging location for deportations – at this point, he had not. However, Turcios had been detained with his passport – another red flag. “[The government] needs two things to remove you: a travel document and a final order of removal,” Copeland says. “They need something to show who you are because in immigration court one of the first things they need to establish is that you’re not a citizen.” If an immigrant picked up by ICE doesn’t have a travel document on them, that buys their attorneys more time.

Meanwhile, Valdivia asked Leah Conklin, another resident who worked in international criminal justice reform, to get involved. Within days of Turcios’s arrest, a crack team was coming together, but time was of the essence. “One of the reasons they make arrests on Friday, I think, is because you can’t catch up,” Valdivia says, “and if you don’t know where they’re going, you don’t know how to stop it.”

Copeland was looking at the online detainee locator system, trying to get a feel for where Turcios was moving – through which processing centre; which detention centre. In New York state, if you are taken to Federal Plaza in Manhattan and then your location “goes dark”, that’s an indicator you could be bound for a deportation flight. “It’s very relevant for filing a habeas petition,” Copeland says, “because you have to file where they’re detained.” If you don’t know where your client is, you can’t file and they can be deported. “So it’s a game they’re playing – hiding the person.”

Conklin had been calling around law firms but found it impossible to get a lawyer quickly enough. On Sunday, Copeland agreed to take on Turcios’s case himself. “I had created the Rapid Defense Network because there’s a small window in which you have to do this. It’s like a death penalty case: you have to strike while the iron’s hot or you’re dead.” By that evening, with Miller’s help, Copeland had filed an emergency petition on Turcios’s behalf, seeking a stay to allow him to consult with lawyers and challenge his removal order. Conklin says that the community came together in record time.

Valdivia messaged some other Rhinebeck residents he knew could amplify Turcios’s story. He called Dunne, the actor and writer who had starred in An American Werewolf in London and After Hours, and whom Valdivia counted as a friend. He texted film-maker Andrew Jarecki, who donated, as did actor Paul Rudd, who co-owns a sweet shop in Rhinebeck and lives there with his family. Word spread. Other contributions came in from all over the US and beyond.

Dunne began posting about Turcios’s case on social media. “It was the first time I’ve ever used Instagram without kind of being embarrassed about self-promotion because I had a movie coming out,” he says. “It made sense to me for the first time. I was just struck by the inhumanity and the contagion of cruelty.”

Friedberg says that when Turcios was arrested, she had a reckoning with herself: “This sort of recognition of how we don’t often know the people that have been working for us or near us for years.” She had never asked about Turcios’s story.

Turcios spent his early childhood in the small town of Balfate on Honduras’s northern coast. His father, Juan, raised cattle. Irma, his mother, gave birth to 10 children. The disappearance of his eldest brother, Amilcar, is one of Turcios’s earliest memories. He was four when his brother went missing after travelling by boat to Roatán, a Honduran island, to seek a better life. Of the five people who made the trip, authorities recovered the bodies of three. Amilcar and the boat’s captain were never found. Turcios’s family never learned the truth; they suspect it had something to do with organised crime, but they’ve come to accept that Amilcar is dead.

While there has been a drop in violent crime in the last couple of years, historically Honduras has been one of the most dangerous countries in the world, with gangs vying for control of drugs and extortion rackets. A decade ago, it frequently topped global lists of the highest murder rates in non-war zone countries, fuelled by its position as a major transit hub for South American cocaine heading to the US.

“My mother was afraid, so she decided we should move from that place where she lost her son,” Turcios says. The family relocated to just outside the large city of San Pedro Sula and stayed there for nine years. Turcios went to school, but eventually they sold up and moved to a house in the mountains. It was beautiful, he says, but dangerous; you could never be sure which was more deadly – the criminal gangs who stole livestock, or the venomous snakes and other wildlife.

They had 10 cows to tend and a few horses, and they began constructing their own house. Laundry was done in a small stream and cooking over fire. Walking to the city took nine hours, over mountain passes; Turcios recalls jumping on his father’s shoulders to cross rivers.

By the time Turcios moved to the mountains, his brother Henoch had already migrated to the US. Henoch says he travelled from Honduras, across Mexico by train, without any money and had to beg for food. He spent three months in Monterrey, where he almost had to have his left hand amputated due to an infection. A friend helped him pay for the medication – the same friend would eventually take in Henoch in Rhinebeck. After he’d recovered enough, he hitched a ride on a train to the border town of Sonoyta, then spent 22 days walking through the southern desert into Arizona. He says he nearly died after spending weeks without eating, surviving on nothing but water.

Eventually, Turcios’s parents decided to move back to town as they wanted his younger sisters, aged eight and 10, to go to school, and to be nearer to a hospital in case they got sick. Turcios stayed in the mountains, living alone for six months so his father wouldn’t have to sell his animals, but he was an hour away by foot from the nearest house. His father gave him a gun for safety and most nights he’d lie awake, clutching it, and listening to the cries of animals in the wilderness.

After the 16-year-old son of his nearest neighbour was murdered over drugs, Turcios’s siblings decided it was time for him to leave Honduras. One day, when visiting his sister in town, he was told that the following morning a man would arrive who would help him cross into Mexico and travel to the US to join his brother. “I didn’t have a future in Honduras,” he says. “If you wanted to go to college, you had to pay a lot of money and my parents couldn’t afford it. And I knew if I went to the United States I would learn how to speak English and it would be better for me.”

Two days later he was travelling across Guatemala by bus and car, under the “care” of a coyote – a people smuggler he had paid 12,000 Honduran pesos, the equivalent of about £350 – or, as he recalls, the amount he’d received for a cow he’d sold five days earlier. Turcios had been told the back route through the mountains would keep him safe. He, his coyote and a group of other migrants moved only at night, but safety proved elusive. At a bus stop in Guatemala, armed officers boarded and ordered passengers to strip. Turcios had hidden his money in his sock, out of sight. The coyote paid the officers off and they kept moving. Hours later, another police stop. This time the driver was pulled from the van, kicked and beaten while officers held a pistol to his head. Only when the driver produced 25,000 Mexican pesos (about £1,000) did they relent.

After 16 nights in a safe house, one migrant demanded better treatment from the people smugglers and that they get moving. Three strangers dragged him outside and he never returned.

The journey took a month and a half. In early December, Turcios and his closest companion, Antonio, were roused at midnight and, together with four others, were packed into a van and dumped in desolate brush. Turcios and Antonio were from the same state in Honduras but hadn’t known each other before. The others were from different countries – El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico. “I was 17. Antonio was 28 and like my older brother,” Turcios says. “His wife and kid had moved to the US a year before and lived in Georgia, so he was trying to reunite with them.”

A guide led them through darkness for 30 minutes. By 3am they had joined 40 others alongside the Rio Grande, shivering in the winter cold. The border was not unguarded. Helicopters buzzed low, forcing them to hide in the grassland and scrub. Mexican army troops encircled them, weapons raised, setting fire to the surrounding brush to flush out the remaining migrants, most of whom fled into the night. Turcios surrendered his pesos and ran. Then, it was time to cross.

After his capture, the US Border Patrol officers took Turcios to a room with a table and two chairs. An officer accused him of being an adult; of running drugs across the border. Turcios told them he was 17, that he had never muled drugs, and that he had gone three days without sleep or food. He produced his birth certificate, which they took and never returned. A doctor arrived, checked his teeth, and confirmed his age. Then the officers stopped yelling, moved him to a cell full of boys his age or younger, and gave him two cookies and a bottle of Kool-Aid – the best meal he had eaten in weeks.

Two days later, he was given new clothes, a jacket for the cold, and told he was flying to New York. It was his first time on a plane, his first time seeing “ice fall from the sky”, as it was snowing that day in New York City. After 26 days in a Long Island shelter, showering each morning and night, and attending a little school inside the facility, he was met by Henoch and Weigel, who drove down from Rhinebeck to collect him.

Six months after Turcios was detained outside his home in Rhinebeck, the campaign to help him had shifted from emergency response to sustained pressure. On a freezing Tuesday afternoon in January, more than 100 students walked out of Rhinebeck’s middle and high schools as part of nationwide anti-ICE protests, defying district policies that required parental permission to leave campus.

My daughter, Scout, then 14, helped organise the walkout, and I watched from the edge of the park as she stood on a podium and told the crowd how ICE had taken a Rhinebeck High School alumnus who had done nothing but contribute to the community and how his detention had affected everyone.

Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random. Last August he was taken to the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, a factory for deportation flights. One morning he was led on to a plane bound for Honduras, but guards pulled him off just before departure after Copeland and other lawyers working on his case won a stay of removal. Over the next 48 hours, Turcios watched as 50 other migrants left the United States, before he was driven back to the detention facility.

In June Turcios had his second court hearing; unlike the first, this one he was required to attend. Dunne says he couldn’t get out of his head the picture of this boy in ankle chains, flanked by guards, looking over at his friends and supporters in the public gallery. “And when he gave us a wave it was just heartbreaking.”

It also brought up traumatic memories. Back in 1982, Dunne’s younger sister, Dominique, died after being strangled by her ex-boyfriend. “The last time I was in a courtroom was over 40 years ago, representing my sister who had been murdered,” he says. “I attended the trial every day … and every day felt like a situation where the system fails you. Seeing Gerson really, really shook me and I thought about things I hadn’t thought about in a long time – that feeling of helplessness.”

On 18 July 2026 Turcios had been in detention for a full year. His fundraiser has reached more than $130,000 in donations from 1,121 different people, but his legal fight continues. After nine years living in Rhinebeck, Henoch self-deported back to Honduras. He says that, given what was happening to Latino people in the US under the Trump administration, he decided it was better to return. “Having to start over here in Honduras is tough, but it has to be done,” he tells me. Today he works on a cattle farm. Henoch’s former girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, still lives in Rhinebeck.

She misses Turcios. “I used to take him everywhere with me. People thought he was my son. I’d tell them he wasn’t, but in the end I just gave up and went with it. He loved to go dancing; he’d try to dance but he wasn’t very good.” She talks to Turcios most nights on the phone. “He’s changed,” she says. “He doesn’t want to admit it, but I think it’s breaking him a little bit.”

Today, now aged 24, Turcios is housed in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn – the same building in which former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and Luigi Mangione, accused of murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City, are awaiting trial. Immigration detainees are kept separate, but are in the same facility.

Turcios says he’s locked in his cell three times a day but allowed out for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and a few hours’ recreation – playing cards, watching TV. “There are four telephones in the unit and we need to line up to use them,” he says. “Sometimes there are eight people waiting and you don’t get to make a call.”

He says the food is bad – breakfast is a packet of milk and a muffin; lunch is pasta with meat that is “old or cold and flavourless”; dinner is mashed potato, spinach and occasionally chicken. “We don’t see sunshine,” he says. “There is a small room where we play basketball and there’s a big opening like a cage, with no glass, and we can see a little piece of the sky.” He speaks to his parents, Irma and Juan, once a week, but calls are expensive – $10 to call Honduras.

Turcios often thinks about how Trump campaigned on deporting all criminal undocumented immigrants. “But the criminals are on the outside,” he says. “And inside, most of these people here with me just came to the United States to work, to try to build our lives and make things better.”

He wants to return to his home in Rhinebeck. “I knew the community was full of incredible, nice people,” Turcios says. “I never expected everyone would get together to help me out. I was so surprised and happy.”

Turcios’s lawyers are challenging his prolonged detention – under a supreme court ruling, the government may detain someone it wants to deport who has a final order of removal for 90 days; between 90 and 180 days, it must show special justification to keep holding them; and after 180 days, it must prove they are “wildly dangerous”. Copeland says this is a level that even a history of gang-related homicide has in the past failed to meet. He argues that Turcios should have been released by October, roughly 90 days into his detention, and that ICE failed to properly notify him of a custody review hearing. In addition, Copeland is pursuing Turcios’s claim for asylum in the US.

Meanwhile, Turcios’s high school friend Anna Lawson, who recently graduated from McGill University in Canada and is taking a gap year before starting law school, is in disbelief that Turcios has been identified by her government as someone who doesn’t belong here. “Gerson is someone who is a benefit to our community and has only enriched it and helped people. I think the American dream really does live in him. He is such an embodiment of what it’s supposed to mean.”

title: Barking up the wrong tree - The Star
description:
For many years, Malaysia hosted refugees from Myanmar who were escaping military oppression and atrocities.
In recent months, rights groups say Rohingya refugees in Malay-sia are facing growing online hate campaigns and disinformation fuelling xenophobia and intimidation.
Last month more than 100 Rohingya refugees gathered outside the UNHCR office in Kuala Lumpur following their relocation from a settlement in Penang.
Does the government think the refugee problem will go away should the UNHCR office close?
Closing down the UNHCR office does not mean ending the refugee problem.
text:
DIPLOMAT Tan Sri Ahmad Kamil Jaafar in his book Growing Up with the Nation (2013), wrote a chapter on the challenges of dealing with the “Boat People” – refugees fleeing a civil war in Vietnam in the 1970s.

Ahmad Kamil, who was in the thick of action back then, shared that the first 47 refugees arrived in Malaysia in May 1975, and the last remaining Vietnamese refugee left Malaysia 30 years later. By then 250,000 refugees had landed in in the country, wrote the former Foreign Ministry’s secretary-general who died in 2021.

At the height of this massive flow, Ahmad Kamil wrote, the domestic political situation in Malaysia was very tense as Malaysians didn’t take kindly to the arrivals and the economic burden they imposed. Interna-tional pressure also existed because Malaysia, which is not a signatory of the 1951 UN Conven-tion Relating to the Status of Refugees, treated the Vietnamese as illegal immigrants, not refugees.

“We could argue that we were free from any obligations to the UN-endorsed 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights and its principle of non-refoulement. But that would make us look callous in the eyes of the world.” Ahmad Kamil wrote.

“We knew that in the final analysis the United Nations was the only organisation with the capacity to resolve this human tragedy. In the end we were vindicated by the successful resettlement of the boat people from our shores through working closely with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the UN.”

(Non-refoulement is a principle of international law that forbids the returning of a victim of persecution to their country.)

Do you feel a sense of deja vu? We are seeing history repeat itself right now.

For many years, Malaysia hosted refugees from Myanmar who were escaping military oppression and atrocities. Following the military coup that overthrew the country’s elected government in 2021, the number of refugees landing on our shores further increased. Most of them are Rohingya Muslims from Rakhine State, long identified as the country’s most persecuted minority.

As of the end of February, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, said there are 215,600 refugees and asylum-seekers registered in Malaysia: 193,824 are from Myanmar, comprising 126,144 Rohingyas, 15,774 Chins, and 33,002 from other ethnic groups from conflict-affected areas of Myanmar.

In recent months, rights groups say Rohingya refugees in Malay-sia are facing growing online hate campaigns and disinformation fuelling xenophobia and intimidation. Last month more than 100 Rohingya refugees gathered outside the UNHCR office in Kuala Lumpur following their relocation from a settlement in Penang. Police said the relocation was prompted by growing competition over economic opportunities and living space following an increase in their numbers.

“They know they are being targeted, so they have to seek protection. Since they are refugees, the government has the obligation to protect them,” said a Malaysian official.

In January, Deputy Foreign Minister Datuk Lukanisman Awang Sauni said a Cabinet decision had been made directing the UNHCR to halt refugee registration temporarily to allow us to set up our own management system, the Refugee Registration Docu-ment (DPP) programme.

His boss, Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan, said Malaysia should reconsider the presence of UNHCR if it refuses to cooperate in implementing a strict screening process for refugee card applicants. Subsequently, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar has agreed to take in ‌5,000 Rohingya asylum seekers currently in Malaysia.

This was followed by Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution’s revelation that his ministry, along with the police and Immigration Department have begun screening Rohingya refugees as part of a process to identify 5,000 Myanmar citizens to be returned to their home country. The screening process would verify the identities and refugee status of those involved.

“The ministry has been tasked, in line with National Security Council Directive No.23, to lead the process with other relevant agencies through the DPP initiative,” he told the media.

The plan has drawn criticism from rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, who are urging Malaysia to reverse course as Rohingya refugees remain at risk of persecution and other serious rights abuses in Myanmar.

The plan then was put on hold when government spokesman Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the government will not repatriate refugees to Myanmar if they still face persecution or risks to their lives.

As the government is working out the finer details of the repatriation, we cannot help but to ask if the UNHCR is assisting the government in this process?

Several years ago a top National Security Council official proposed closing the UNHCR office to allow Putrajaya to manage refugees in the country better without “interference” from external influences. He had acknowledged that this could not be done so soon as a management mechanism must be in place.

Before we argue whether the UNHCR should shut down its office here, maybe we should ask ourselves who invited the UN agency to set up in the country?

Secondly, if Myanmar refuses to accept its own people, what is the guarantee that we can send them to third countries? Do we have a bilateral agreement with any recipient countries? There is already fatigue among many countries in opening their borders to refugees. Western Europe is facing an influx of immigrants from North Africa.

In the case of the boat people, the United States was involved in the war in Vietnam so, naturally, it had to accept the refugees from there.

It is easy to say refugees come to Malaysia because the UNHCR office is here, but we cannot ignore that our location, stability, and, to a certain extent, wealth have made us an attractive destination for refugees and illegal immigrants from around the region.

If the government is seeking cooperation from the UN agency as the Foreign Minister said, what kind of cooperation is it seeking?

Does the government think the refugee problem will go away should the UNHCR office close?

Does Malaysia have an existing law defining a refugee and a process to identify and verify one, including whether that process is internationally recognised?

What about those seeking political asylum? This is a separate case from that of a refugee. There must also be a clear distinction between genuine refugees, those seeking political asylum, and illegal immigrants.

We understand the government’s frustration that resettlement has been very slow but it is myopic to think Malaysia can resolve the refugee problem without involving the UNHCR.

Perhaps the government should continue working with the UNCHR office by collaborating properly with the agency until such time we can manage the refugees ourselves with a system that is recognised by the international community.

This is a very complex issue. If this is about our national security, then we need to better protect our land and maritime borders.

Once refugees – and this doesn’t just apply to the Rohingya – enter our territory, they become our obligation whether we like it or not, and regardless of whether we ratify the 1951 UN Convention.

Closing down the UNHCR office does not mean ending the refugee problem.

Haworth's analogy about immigrants was wrong

DEAR EDITOR:

I really have to disagree with Ian Haworth's editorial printed on Monday, July 6, regarding the Supreme Court's decision to uphold birthright citizenship. He uses a very poor and purposely slanted analogy of he and his wife breaking into a neighbor's home, having a baby in the home and then forcing the parents in that home to raise the child. In the analogy, he also mentions that he and his wife are "rifling through your fridge."

The majority of immigrants into the US want to raise their own families and contrary to Mr. Haworth's analogy of "rifling through the fridge," the majority of the immigrants are working and contributing to the economy.

The Trump administration's dislike of immigrants is about hatred, not security. Spending $70 billion to deport immigrants, even if they are illegal, leaves the US with nothing – and could aggravate inflation -- for that investment. Giving working immigrants a path to citizenship is a far better investment since it grows the economy by adding consumers and labor to the economy.

Any nation that is great enough to attract immigrants is being given a gift. Most immigrants are considered illegal because Congress has failed to create a viable immigration policy. Many immigrants leave everything behind coming with little or nothing. They are willing to work and build a life for themselves and their children.

My grandfather left Italy at age 17, came here with nothing but what he could carry. He didn't know the language; he didn't have any money; he didn't have a job. But he was willing to work. He found his way to Herminie, PA and worked on a farm. Recalled to Italy to fight in the Italian Navy in WWI, he met my grandmother after the war and returned to the US. My grandparents raised five siblings. His work ethic rubbed off on my dad who taught me the value of work and earning your own way. I can guarantee you that my life is orders of magnitude better because of my grandfather's bravery in coming to the US as an immigrant.

Let's give immigrants who want to be here and who are not serious criminals a path to citizenship. Hatred begets more hatred, and hatred will destroy us.

Thank you for your assistance. Have a good summer!

DAVID J. BISIGNANI

Austintown

The war isn't in Iran; it's in Youngstown

DEAR EDITOR:

This is brother Abdul Harris, lifelong fed up resident of the city of Youngstown, where these inept leaders say it's safe to live here. No, how about it's safe to die here! Houses getting shot up, Young dude last week shot to death on the South Side and juveniles shooting gel guns at parishioners at church. Come on! And in the Brier Hill area over the weekend, you guessed it, shooting down there too!

Yet these leftover leaders that did much of nothing under the lame eight-year tyranny of the last leader here, most are still in power doing nothing to quell these senseless killings/shootings. Oh, where is that impact initiative, Mr. Mayor? And who gave a certain group a permit last Saturday to block the streets Lansing and East High on the neglected lower First Ward? For nine hours straight we the people had to endure this wretched music shaking our homes. Mind you we're elderly and seniors from ages 55 to 95 and did anyone from this organization or anyone from y'all precious downtown notify any of us that this was going on?

Remember this, you lame leaders when election -- I mean selection -- time comes up and we the people add the name Sike to the ballot!

ABDUL HARRIS

Youngstown

Section 219 of the NDAA goes too far

DEAR EDITOR:

One of my new concerns is the National Defense Authorization Act. Section 219 was slipped into this 1,000-page, excessive bill. Section 219 will allow Israel's Netanyahu to have access to our military information and our money. It will merge Israel and U.S. forces.

My opinion is not about antisemitism, which I totally oppose. This is about keeping our country free -- free from Israel merging into our military; using our money; our resources and intelligence information, which would include, electronic warfare, directed energy and biotechnology use. This law would limit our congressional oversight of wars in which we would then be entangled. Netanyahu is a "never end wars" kind of guy.

This bill has passed the House and is now in the Senate. Please call our senators to stop this bill from moving forward. If it passes, it will become law and the U.S. and Israel will have merged our troops and, "Our taxed based" military spending.

The 2027 budget for war spending is set at an all-time high $1.5 trillion! A better use of much of this money would be to provide affordable health care; food for those who need it; improving our educational systems; affordable housing and meeting more basic needs for our country. Not war! Our funding for food programs alone has been cut by $63 billion!

This law would have another warring country have access to all our military information and allow them to use our tax dollars for their war interests. We do not need to be merged with Genocidal Netanyahu. Please call our senators, and urge them to oppose the National Defense Authorization Act, especially Section 219. Call Sen. Bernie Moreno at 202-224-2315 and Sen. Jon Husted at 202-224-3353.

ELIZABETH BRAHAM

North Lima

The jokes' landing all depends on the delivery

DEAR EDITOR:

A new arrival at the penitentiary on his first day of entertainment hour. Inmates gathered in a large auditorium for a banter event. One inmate gets on a stage and starts calling out number 5143, and all the inmates applaud.

The new inmate is puzzled. A second inmate gets up on the stage; he calls out 7361. Again, all the inmates applaud.

Finally, the new inmate inquired about this strange happening.

The odd times explain the situation. These men had been in there so long they knew all the jokes. To keep it brief, they just called out numbers to represent the jokes. The old-timer suggested the new inmate try it.

The new inmate got on the stage repeating the numbers that got the most applause.

"5143." The audience went silent.

Baffled, he asked the old-timer what had happened.

His response was, "Some people can tell them; some people can't."

Kamala Harris eyes a possible 2028 comeback. As a whole, the nation goes silent.

PAUL R. LAWSON

McDonald

Poland Village Assisted Living has gone overboard

DEAR EDITOR:

Families pay thousands of dollars for senior care, yet Poland Village Assisted Living is telling vulnerable residents they must now provide their own toilet paper, tissues and trash bags.

Many of these seniors have no local family and cannot physically shop for themselves. Cutting off basic hygiene essentials is a cruel way to boost profit margins.

Management needs to reverse this decision and put resident care over corporate greed.

When will you realize that Trump doesn't care?

DEAR EDITOR:

Trump "seems" to be all powerful now; he could almost fly around the world screaming, "I am the King of the World," BUT … tiny cracks are appearing in his crown. However, he still does whatever he wants, still doesn't seem to care what is happening in the U.S. or its citizens, and spends money, our money not his, on self-aggrandizements.

He has canceled the ACA for millions of Americans. He is cutting Medicare's drug subsidies despite telling us he could lower the cost of drugs "1400%!" (which is impossible). Other insurance companies have joined in by raising the cost to impossible levels. If I didn't know better I "could" think he wants Americans (unimportant ones) to die off. Yet many refuse to understand that he really simply does not care. Not a good move and is angering many.

He and Vance urge young parents to have more babies. Many are barely able to afford the family they have now. If he thought the $1,000 he would give new parents would help, he is seriously out of touch .. .which actually he is.

Rent, food, medicines, utilities, insurance, clothing … every facet of American lives' needs are coming up short. Add in poor pay at 1970 levels. Mortgages are in jeopardy. He really does not care.

With millions of people fired from federal positions, shutting of agencies, departments, top positions, and more, where is this extra cash? He has actually added several Trillions to the national debt. War is expensive. He just doesn't care.

He doesn't like "affordability." "Groceries" was an unfamiliar word to him.

I was under the impression that a president was elected as head of ALL states, not just red. That help would go to ALL states. Right now help is needed for massive fires in the state of Washington. Will he send help? Usually, well actually before Trump, when any disaster happens the president issues some words of condolence, and then assures that help is on the way. Not Trump, he says fires won't happen if you rake the leaves in the forest so they don't catch fire. Who thinks this? A compassionate man? I don't think so, but a man consumed with himself, and one who really doesn't care what happens to the people as long as he gets what he wants. It is all about him.

JEANNE McDERMOTT

Liberty

Let's look at the facts about Dr. Amy Acton

DEAR EDITOR:

I am very disturbed and angered by the television ads about Amy Acton. They are nasty and visually distorted, AI-generated. They contain lies, half-truths and innuendoes.

Dr. Acton had a very rough childhood. She was homeless, lived briefly in a tent during the winter, and was sexually abused as a child. If you research her life, you will find that the one supposed drinking/drug incident has been blown all out of proportion and exaggerated.

Given her background, it would be surprising if she didn't have PTSD. She has risen far above her horribly difficult beginnings. I greatly admire her.

The ads accuse her of shutting down Ohio during COVID. She did not have the power to do that. She was an ADVISER, as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, to Gov. Mike DeWine. He made informed decisions about closures, masks, vaccines, etc. Ohio fared better than many states in death rates and recovery.

Dr. Acton has had a career giving to others. Her credentials are impressive -- Doctor of Medicine from Northeastern Ohio College of Medicine and a Master's Degree in Public Health. She was the Woman of the Year for Ohio and won the Profile in Courage Award in 2022, among her many recognitions and awards. Her focus has long been on public health and wellness.

Dr. Acton cares!

Contrast Dr. Acton with Vivek Ramaswamy. His bio does not include any mention of a public office. He has degrees from Harvard and Yale Law School. He is worth 2.8 billion. As of 2024 he has moved his company, FINANCIAL SERVICES Strive Enterprises, to Dallas. He is funded by $25 million of his own money and millions from Elon Musk and others of the billionaire class.

Why is he running? Perhaps, like Trump and Elon, he plans to make billions more. Which person will have your welfare in mind?

BECKY MURRAY

Poland

Desperate Republicans are playing the communist card

DEAR EDITOR:

Donald Trump, Mike Johnson and other prominent Republicans have, out of some sort of desperation, I assume, begun calling liberal Democrats "communists."

Liberal Democrats embrace the civil rights of all individuals, the sanctity of free speech, adherence to the rule of law, the rights of all citizens to expect free and fair elections and the protection of citizens against abuse by the government.

I challenge those Republicans to find any communist government, or member of any communist party that support those same ideals. The only thing more stupid than this idiotic name-calling by Republicans would be the people who believe the stupidity.

THOMAS BRENT

MADRID (AP) — A diplomatic spat between Spain and Italy over the rush of tens of thousands of migrants to the Spanish territory of Ceuta escalated on Saturday after the government in Madrid announced border controls on Italian travelers in response to Rome's decision to impose sanctions on visitors from Spain.

Italians arriving at Barcelona airport were subject to random police checks after the controls were put into effect overnight, according to Spain’s state news agency EFE.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The Spanish government said the controls would stay in place for at least a month after Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni rejected Spain’s warning on Friday that it would take “proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens” if Rome didn’t lift its own restrictions by an Aug. 9 deadline.

Italy began enforcing air and sea border controls on Spanish citizens on Aug. 1 following Meloni’s scathing criticism of the progressive migration policies of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

The feud was triggered after the sudden arrival of 72,000 migrants from Morocco at Spain’s North African territory late last month. Although most of the migrants have since gone back, more than 80 migrants died, including some who drowned or were trampled in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier, according to Spanish and Moroccan authorities.

The migrant rush on Ceuta also reignited the immigration debate within the European Union, whose leaders criticized Sanchez for policies that they suggested were responsible for the massive influx.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Hawkish EU leaders like Meloni pointed to such policies, including a Spanish government decision to carry out an amnesty for immigrants without residency permits who could prove they had been living in the country for at least five months and arrived before Jan. 1 this year. Over 1 million people applied before the window closed at the end of last month.

The 27-member EU bloc has a visa-free travel area known as Schengen that allows citizens of most EU countries to travel easily across borders for work and pleasure.

According to the EU, member states are allowed to temporarily reintroduce controls at the EU’s so-called internal borders in case of a serious threat, such as one to internal security. But it also says border controls should be applied as a last resort in exceptional situations, and must be time-limited.

Meloni’s office on Friday said Italian authorities “have no intention” of lifting border checks on people arriving from Spain by sea or air until at least Aug. 15 — six days after the Spanish deadline.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad about national security and border control,” a statement said.

Should there be a repeat of migrant arrivals in Ceuta, Italy would review its decision to impose the checks “only when we are certain that there will be no security or terrorist risks for Italy, that there will be no new wave, and that there are no irregular migrants heading towards European territory,” the statement added.

text:
YOU MIGHT THINK DEMOCRATS would be up in arms over the violence perpetrated by the Trump administration and its agencies in implementing its deportation agenda.

And on its official social media channels, the Democratic party has issued powerful statements, as well as posts highlighting the last words of those killed by state violence.

But a closer look reveals that that social media energy has not translated into actual midterm messaging.

On July 26, less than two weeks after Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero’s death in Maine, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries unveiled the party’s “Fighting for an Affordable America” agenda in Pennsylvania alongside Gov. Josh Shapiro. The program made clear how the Democrats are framing the run-in to the midterms, with a focus on pocketbook issues such as (in the AP’s summary) “restoring healthcare cuts, bringing the cost of living down and ending the war in Iran to beat Republicans and hold President Donald Trump accountable.”

Glaringly absent from the Democratic priorities: reining in ICE abuses.

Again, it’s not that Democrats aren’t aware of the case for urgent action on Trump’s deportation regime. Privately, immigration advocacy groups have been pushing for them to speak out. Just four days before Jeffries’s agenda unveiling and before the August recess, a hundred Democratic members of Congress were briefed on the stakes of—and the electoral opportunity in—facing Trump’s brutal anti-immigrant program head-on.

During a weekly meeting convened by Rep. Katherine Clark, the House Democratic whip, Todd Schulte and Maria Praeli of the immigration-advocacy group FWD.us encouraged House Dems to meet the moment by “confronting anti-immigrant actions and violence.” Their PowerPoint presentation, obtained by The Bulwark, contends that the country has undergone a transformation on immigration in the last year, making immigration a viable, even critical, electoral issue that Democrats must seize upon heading into this fall’s midterms.

Schulte and Praeli told the Democratic lawmakers that forcing a government shutdown fight over Department of Homeland Security funding after the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis—and linking immigration enforcement overreach and waste with affordability in general—was a political success, reinforcing voters’ growing belief that Trump’s priorities are warped.

They also highlighted that ICE’s exorbitant funding extends well past Trump’s term into 2029. And not only that—with the money that Congress has appropriated for it, the agency could actually continue to run at fiscal year 2025 levels well past the end of the decade, with enough cash to keep going “without [receiving] another dime until 2033.” Schulte and Praeli emphasized that ICE is toxic among voters: Citing data from the progressive polling firm Navigator showing ICE at its lowest net approval rating this spring, even before its recent Houston and Maine killings, which they linked to the $270 billion it received in federal funding.

The pair recommended a range of action items for Democrats to profitably focus attention on immigration, including advising them to:

mention specific stories of individuals who have been here for decades and are caught in the Trump administration dragnet,

continue to tie immigration overreach and corruption to affordability concerns,

hold more detention center visits,

conduct field hearings, and

participate in national days of action for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Guerrero.

The advice for Democrats to go on the strategic offensive on immigration was offered in part to further shake the party out of its post–2024 election paralysis. Back then, Democrats felt that they had completely missed where Americans were on questions of border security and immigration. That uncertainty led to awkward strategic silences and a lack of coherent strategy in response to the early ramp-up of Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

During those bleak months, Democrats regularly assured me that Trump would go too far and a messaging opening would appear, but until that happened, they and their colleagues were frozen.

Trump did go too far, and some of the administration’s most egregious actions chipped away at voter trust in the president and his party on immigration. The presentation reminded lawmakers of the litany of DHS scandals and outrages over the last year and a half, including the time Kilmar Ábrego Garcia was mistakenly sent to a torture prison in El Salvador, and the multiple invasions of American cities, which started with federal agents descending on Los Angeles last summer and eventually resulted in shocking deaths in Minneapolis and elsewhere.

The proof is in the polling. A Fox News survey from mid-July shows voters now trust Democrats on immigration more than they do Republicans, eating into a previously winning issue for the GOP.

The party’s left flank long ago began to heed the call to push back against Trump more assertively on immigration, but their more moderate colleagues have often seemed more hesitant. Chris Newman, legal director of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON) and an attorney for Ábrego García, published an opinion article this week titled “Trump’s Immigration Policies Have Been Rejected; Why Won’t Dems Act Like It?”

Newman argued that Trump was always going to fail on immigration, and Democrats, too cowed to speak up in March 2025, now have an opportunity to do so with voter winds in their sails.

“Democratic elites should join the grassroots in fighting the real adversary—the brutal, violent, white-nationalist deportation campaign now tearing this country apart. They should get out of their conference rooms and Zoom calls and hit the streets with us,” he wrote.

Newman praised Democrats like Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) who went to El Salvador to meet with Ábrego García, as well as Reps. Joaquin Castro, who fought for the release of children and families from the detention center in Dilley, Texas, and Sylvia Garcia (D-Tex.), who stood with Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s family after his killing in Houston. There were others, too, like Sen. Andy Kim and Reps. LaMonica McIver and Rob Menendez, who fought against the abuses of Delaney Hall, a detention center in their state of New Jersey.

“Every Democrat should do the same,” Newman wrote. “Not as a photo op, but because it’s right. And because in every election to come, Democrats will be judged not by their campaign promises, but by what they did in the years Trump was in office.”

Share

The False Choice Between Fighting ICE and Winning Elections

Still, a good chunk of the Democratic party seems to remain in that state of paralysis. In reporting this story, I heard over and over from Democrats involved in tight races that while immigration is a top-polling issue across the country, campaigns weren’t willing to risk advertising on it, especially now that we’re just three months out from November’s general election. Putting campaign dollars into anti-ICE messaging is still considered too much of a gamble.

“It was everywhere in the primary. When it was Dem-on-Dem, every Democrat was using immigration and ICE as a cudgel,” one strategist involved in more than fifteen Democratic races across the country told me. “Now in the general, pollsters do a poll and immigration shows up as a top-three issue, but Democrats are scared to talk about it because they think it’s going to turn off Trump voters, and they’re wrong.”

The pattern often becomes visible in local races, where money is tight, and campaign teams prefer to spend it on safe and reliable messaging on economic issues and Trump’s corruption rather than gambling it by crafting anti-ICE ads or making immigration policy pronouncements. That dynamic has been reinforced by outside PACs and groups, who can’t coordinate with the campaigns directly on messaging, and so need to take their cues from what the campaign prioritizes publicly. That coordination-by-another-name works easiest when the campaign’s messaging is most familiar to everyone involved.

Not all Democrats are locked into the old patterns. Manny Rutinel, a 31-year-old Colorado state House member running for Congress in the hypercompetitive 8th district, which the Cook Political Report rates a tossup, has put immigration at the center of his campaign. During the primary, he picked it up and used it to hammer his opponent Shannon Bird over an ICE-in-sensitive-locations bill; he clobbered her by 28 points. Rutinel is still talking immigration, now in the context of the general election, which he hopes to win to represent the most Hispanic congressional district in Colorado. Rutinel makes his priorities clear on the front page of his website: An inscription there reads, “I’m running to represent Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, and I’m fighting to lower costs, stop ICE from terrorizing our communities, and stand up to Trump’s attacks on our rights.”

“There was a bill where we came together to be able to stop ICE from going into schools and hospitals,” Rutinel told me, recounting his work in the state legislature:

It was a clear demonstration that Donald Trump isn’t interested in safety. What he’s doing here is targeting women and children, and terrifying our communities. . . . I highlighted that bill because there was a contrast there. It’s personal for me as a son of an immigrant in a district that is 40 percent Latino.

While few districts nationwide have such high Latino populations, Rutinel’s approach could still be adapted to campaigns in other parts of the country. He told me the people of his district feel betrayed by Trump for failing to follow through on his promise to go after violent criminals and instead tearing families apart.

“Folks are feeling the whole thing is being mismanaged. The focus is not on things they want the Trump administration to focus on. Folks across this district can’t afford rent,” he added, before lumping Trump and his opponent Gabe Evans together: “If they spent as much time thinking about lowering costs as they do about tormenting immigrants, things would be less expensive.”

Colin Rogero, a Democratic admaker who worked on two immigration-related ads hitting Bird for Somos PAC, a Latino voter-engagement group that backed Rutinel, told me Democrats can’t allow Republicans to define the playing field on immigration.

“It moves us enough to the right that it has voters asking what the difference is between us and Republicans when we’re taking money from the same people,” he said. “They shouldn’t just be killing and jailing people indiscriminately, but who is saying we have to stand up and fight that? It has to be us as a party.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement says all of its field officers will soon wear body cameras, but a policy governing the devices gives the agency broad discretion over whether the public gets to see what they record.

ICE plans to equip officers nationwide with body-worn cameras by the end of September, following mounting scrutiny over fatal encounters involving federal immigration officers. But footage from shootings or incidents resulting in death or serious injury will be released promptly only when ICE determines doing so is in the agency’s “best interests,” according to the policy.

After a serious incident, a committee composed of senior ICE officials and attorneys will review the footage and recommend whether it should be released. Video could be made public within 72 hours, but the ICE director can delay or block its release if there are “specific and compelling circumstances.” The policy does not define what those circumstances are.

The rollout follows several fatal encounters involving immigration officers, including the deaths of two men shot by ICE agents in Texas and Maine last month. Neither shooting was captured on an officer’s body camera. Civilian video has also played a significant role in challenging official accounts of other controversial immigration enforcement encounters.

Experts say ICE’s control over which recordings become public could undermine the accountability the cameras are intended to provide.

“In some ways, ICE is saying the quiet part out loud,” Christopher Schneider, a sociology professor who studies police body cameras, told The Associated Press, describing selective release policies as a way for law enforcement agencies to shape their public image.

The Brennan Center for Justice has similarly warned that the effectiveness of body cameras depends heavily on the policies governing their use, including when cameras must be activated, whether footage is publicly accessible and what happens when officers fail to follow the rules. Research into body cameras has produced mixed results on whether they reduce use of force, though some studies have found reductions in complaints against officers.

Start your day with essential news from Salon.

Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

ICE spent $30.9 million on body-camera equipment in July, according to federal records cited by AP. Congress had previously allocated another $20 million for the cameras.

Tom Homan, President Donald Trump’s border czar, has defended the expansion, saying body cameras frequently exonerate law enforcement officers and would allow Americans to “see what the officers saw.”

Whether Americans will actually get to see that footage, however, may ultimately remain ICE’s decision.

text:
Denver — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet joined Senator John Hickenlooper and Colorado U.S. Representatives Jason Crow, Diana DeGette, Joe Neguse, and Brittany Pettersen in a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding answers following last month’s shooting by a GEO Group employee near the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Aurora that left one person injured. The lawmakers also called for a thorough review of the Department’s policies to help prevent similar incidents.

The letter seeks answers about DHS and ICE’s coordination with local law enforcement, employee training, contractor vetting, security protocols, and the steps the agencies are taking to strengthen oversight and prevent harmful incidents.

“We write to express our concern over the July 16, 2026 shooting of a 21-year-old woman near the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Aurora, Colorado. While we are relieved that her injuries were not life-threatening, we must ensure that personnel operating at federal immigration detention facilities are adequately screened and trained to prevent incidents like this one,” wrote the lawmakers.

“The incident in Aurora, and the broader pattern of shootings involving Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personnel across the country, undermine public trust and threaten community safety. As members of the Colorado Congressional delegation, we are responsible for defending the constitutional rights of our constituents and protecting our communities and our law enforcement. The events in Aurora raise questions about whether current DHS policies and practices keep communities, protesters, and law enforcement safe. We believe a thorough review of the Department’s policies is necessary to ensure that similar incidents do not recur,” continued the lawmakers.

Bennet has consistently fought against the Trump administration’s inhumane immigration policies. In July, Bennet joined U.S. Senator Angus King (I-Maine) and 37 of their Senate colleagues in calling for stronger accountability measures for ICE officers. In May 2026, Bennet introduced three bills aimed at reforming the DHS, including ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP): the Keeping Immigrants and Destinations Safe (KIDS) Act; the Training, Responsibility, Uniforms, and Standards for Transparency (TRUST) Act; and the Oversight, Protection, and Enforcement Notification (OPEN) Act.

In March 2026, Bennet issued a statement when Trump fired former Secretary Noem, and emphasized that DHS must undergo a complete overhaul, which is only the first step toward DHS reforms. In January 2026, Bennet joined his colleagues in introducing the Providing Useful Budgets for Localities to Invest in Cops by Substituting Appropriations from Federal Enforcement To Yield Results (PUBLIC SAFETY) Act, legislation to redirect nearly $75 billion in funding passed in the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act from ICE and send it instead to local law enforcement programs to help hire and train 200,000 local police officers in communities across the country.

In November 2025, Bennet joined his colleagues in introducing the bicameral Restoring Access to Detainees Act, legislation to ensure DHS allows noncitizens who have been detained to contact their legal counsel and families. In August 2025, he joined the Immigration Enforcement Identification Safety Act to prohibit immigration enforcement officials from wearing masks and to require them to wear visible identification. In February 2025, Bennet joined his Senate colleagues to introduce the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would reinstate DHS’ long-standing policies to prevent ICE from making arrests at sensitive locations like schools, hospitals, and places of worship.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Mullin:

We write to express our concern over the July 16, 2026 shooting of a 21-year-old woman near the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Aurora, Colorado. While we are relieved that her injuries were not life-threatening, we must ensure that personnel operating at federal immigration detention facilities are adequately screened and trained to prevent incidents like this one. According to the Aurora Police Department, GEO Group employees reporting for their shifts that day were unable to enter the facility because of protest activity. Police allege that two protesters verbally confronted GEO employees and photographed their vehicles before walking away. One employee then retrieved a personally owned firearm and fired in their direction, striking one woman in the foot. He has been charged with seven offenses, including attempted second-degree murder.

Immigration enforcement officers and the contractors supporting them have an obligation to protect public safety while exercising restraint and professionalism. Protests outside immigration detention centers are routine occurrences. An agency responsible for operating secure facilities should be equipped to maintain safe access, communicate with employees, coordinate with local law enforcement, and prevent confrontations between the community and facility personnel from escalating. Just as we believe law enforcement should never be targeted with violence, we believe lawful protesters should be protected – not attacked – by federal officials or those contracted by the government.

The incident in Aurora, and the broader pattern of shootings involving Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personnel across the country, undermine public trust and threaten community safety. As members of the Colorado Congressional delegation, we are responsible for defending the constitutional rights of our constituents and protecting our communities and our law enforcement. The events in Aurora raise questions about whether current DHS policies and practices keep communities, protesters, and law enforcement safe. We believe a thorough review of the Department’s policies is necessary to ensure that similar incidents do not recur.

Given this urgent need, we request written responses to the following questions by August 14, 2026:

What coordination has DHS and ICE undertaken with state and local law enforcement to manage public demonstrations while ensuring employees can safely access their places of work? What will that coordination look like moving forward?

What de-escalation, use-of-force, crisis intervention, threats against employees, and crowd-management training is required for DHS personnel and contractor employees assigned to ICE facilities? What training has been provided to the employees at the Aurora facility concerning de-escalation, use-of-force, crisis intervention, threats against employees, and crowd-management training? Which of these trainings did the employee charged in the July 16 shooting complete and on which dates did he complete them?

What screening and vetting procedures does DHS require for contractor personnel before they are assigned to ICE facilities? What screening was conducted for the individual charged in the July 16 shooting?

What policies and operational plans do DHS and ICE have in place to protect both protesters and employees outside DHS and ICE facilities, including contracted facilities? Does ICE require its detention contractors to designate alternative entrances, transportation arrangements, or other measures for employees during demonstrations or other disruptions to access?

GEO Group has placed the employee on unpaid leave and stated that it is cooperating with law enforcement. Beyond the ongoing investigation, what additional steps will DHS and ICE take to determine whether similar vulnerabilities exist at other contracted detention facilities? How will DHS and ICE strengthen oversight of its personnel and contractors and prevent similar incidents from occurring?

In addition to providing the information above, we urge the Department to conduct an independent review of its security procedures, contractor oversight, employee training, and firearms policies, especially as they relate to anticipated confrontations, and to make its findings and recommendations publicly available.

We appreciate your prompt attention to this urgent matter and look forward to your response.

text:
The state of New Jersey announced an investigation into the state's largest immigration detention center, Delaney Hall, located in the city of Newark.

The investigation targets GEO Group, a private company that manages detention facilities and prisons under government contracts. In this case, it is the company contracted to operate the Delaney Hall facility, where U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detains immigrants.

Specifically, the New Jersey Civil Rights Division issued subpoenas to determine whether GEO Group employees violated the civil rights of immigrants detained at the center.

"New Jersey has a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people in our State. For detained individuals, including those held by a private corporation like GEO Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care," stated Jennifer Davenport, New Jersey's attorney general, in a press release.

"We will take every action available under law to safeguard these core legal principles. We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected," she added.

In turn, Davenport's office reported that, if the investigation determines that violations occurred, legal action could be taken "under the New Jersey Civil Rights Act (NJCRA) and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD)."

Delaney Hall had previously been the scene of clashes with federal agents

Delaney Hall previously made headlines in May, when protesters clashed with federal agents during demonstrations against ICE operations in the city. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka was arrested during one of those incidents.

text:
Gabriel Johnson's relatives say the 55-year-old remains partially paralyzed as they continue fighting for his release and access to rehabilitation following his medical emergency.

The family of Gabriel Johnson, the North Carolina pastor who suffered a stroke while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, has finally been able to see him as they continue pushing for his release and answers about the medical care he received while detained.

Johnson, a 55-year-old Liberian immigrant who has lived legally in the United States since he was 15, was taken into ICE custody from his family's home in Cary, North Carolina, on July 15. Since then, he has been moved through detention facilities in multiple states, ultimately arriving in Texas, where his family says he suffered a stroke on July 30.

NBC News reported Saturday that Johnson's relatives recently traveled to Texas and were permitted to visit him after previously struggling to gain access to him following his hospitalization. According to accounts shared by the family, the visit lasted about an hour.

His family says Johnson remains paralyzed on one side of his body and faces a significant recovery.

The visit marks the latest development in a case that has drawn attention to medical care inside the federal immigration detention system and left Johnson's family fighting on several fronts at once. They are seeking his release so that he can begin rehabilitation while also questioning whether his stroke could have been prevented.

As theGrio previously reported, Johnson has a history of high blood pressure and previous minor strokes. His daughter, Gabri Johnson, said her father repeatedly told relatives during his detention that he was not consistently receiving his prescribed medication, adequate food or water. The family alleges those conditions contributed to his deteriorating health before his stroke.

ICE has described Johnson as a Liberian national targeted as part of an immigration enforcement operation. His family, however, stresses that he came to the United States as a teenager, has maintained legal status for decades and built his life in North Carolina, where he became an ordained pastor, husband and father of four.

Johnson is also a graduate of North Carolina Central University, a historically Black university in Durham.

The circumstances surrounding his detention have become part of his family's broader demand for transparency. A federal habeas corpus petition challenging Johnson's detention was filed on July 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia, where he had been detained before being transferred to Texas.

His relatives have also sought an emergency stay of removal, arguing that Johnson needs time in the United States to receive medical care and rehabilitation before any immigration proceedings move forward.

The family's concerns intensified after his hospitalization. They said they initially had difficulty communicating directly with Johnson or obtaining information about his location. His daughter previously said a hospital contacted the family to tell them he had suffered a stroke, but they were not immediately able to freely communicate with him.

Now that family members have seen him in person, their focus remains on getting him out of federal custody and into rehabilitation.

The case comes amid broader scrutiny of health and safety conditions within the rapidly expanding U.S. immigration detention system. In North Carolina, the federal government is also moving toward expanding detention capacity, including plans involving the former Rivers Correctional Institution in Hertford County. State and immigrant-rights advocates have raised concerns about medical care, oversight and conditions as detention capacity grows.

For Johnson's family, however, the policy debate has become deeply personal.

Their father entered ICE custody in mid-July, able to communicate with them and manage his existing medical conditions. Weeks later, they are trying to secure rehabilitation for a man they say is now living with the physical effects of a major stroke.

And while finally being able to sit with him offered the family something they had been fighting for since his hospitalization, their larger fight is far from over.

They want him home.
