text:
The Trump administration is once again trying to limit who can become an American, with a pair of executive orders issued this week that attempt to place restrictions on birthright citizenship and on foreigners who give birth in the U.S.

WATCH: Trump signs executive orders imposing new limits on birthright citizenship

A Supreme Court decision in June struck down a previous attempt at restricting birthright citizenship, but Thursday's orders were made with "adjustments" keeping the decision in mind, President Donald Trump said.

Still, some of the restrictions announced by the White House are expected to face legal challenges.

The 14th Amendment, which makes a citizen of anyone born in the country, and two subsequent Supreme Court decisions interpreting it provide guidelines that already exclude certain births from receiving the citizenship benefit.

Trump's new attempt to restrict birthright citizenship even after the Supreme Court loss highlights the administration's drive to limit who can become an American.

New categories of restricted citizenship benefits

Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions.

The executive order released Thursday was narrower in scope than the previous one shot down by the Supreme Court and appeared to focus on restricting automatic citizenship to specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations as well as anyone considered an "alien enemy" of the United States.

WATCH: Examining the Supreme Court's birthright citizenship, campaign finance rulings

U.S. immigration law says babies born to a "foreign diplomatic officer accredited to the United States" are not entitled to birthright citizenship under the Constitution, including ambassadors, ministers, chargés d'affaires, counselors, secretaries and attachés of embassies and legations, and members of the Delegation of the Commission of the European Communities.

Trump's orders Thursday would sharply expand those exemptions.

One order disqualifies babies who are products of "birth tourism." The other applies to children of anyone working in a foreign embassy or representing a foreign government and employees of the United Nations or other international organizations. Children of parents tied to groups that are deemed terrorist organizations, like Antifa or Tren de Aragua, are also excluded.

"How is the federal government going to decide that a child is born to a member of a designated terrorist organization?" said César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, a law professor at Ohio State University. "These are not organizations that are sharing the membership lists if they even have them."

Citizenship through surrogacy has become a concern for Republican members of Congress, some of whom proposed a bill this year that would restrict citizenship for children of noncitizen parents born to surrogates in the U.S.

García Hernández said he believes the new executive order addressing surrogacy could raise new legal questions. "Neither the 14th Amendment nor any of the Supreme Court's decisions about how to interpret the 14th Amendment mentions or hints at surrogates," the law professor said.

Questions over the scope of birth tourism

Trump's executive order defines birth tourism as someone who enters the United States on a "nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil."

Birth tourism is already considered fraud and grounds to restrict a visa if someone seeks one specifically to come to the U.S. and obtain citizenship for a child.

Advocates said the executive order would give immigration officers discretion to deny entry to pregnant women suspected of wanting to give birth in the U.S. without providing clearly defined guidelines.

READ MORE: Fact-checking the Trump administration's challenges to birthright citizenship

The president did not offer data indicating the scope of the problem, but said Thursday: "I'll tell you right now, hundreds of thousands, OK? Hundreds of thousands."

Although there's no official estimate of how many births can be considered "birth tourism" cases, experts say Trump's approximation is exaggerated.

"The hundreds of thousands just seems like an overestimate based on the sort of limited data that we have available," said Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute.

Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that in 2024 nearly 9,600 children were born to foreign mothers with an official address outside the country. Another estimate from the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that advocates for lower immigration, estimated that 20,000 to 26,000 birth tourists come to the U.S. each year.

Facilitators of birth tourism targeted

The order provides a sweeping indictment of "birth tourism operators" with no evidence of how widespread they are or how or why anyone accused of using their services would be exempt from constitutional protection.

Those efforts are not new either. Previous administrations have also sought to prosecute so-called "birth tourism" schemes that helped women hide their pregnancies while traveling to the United States to give birth.

"Birth tourism operators use deceptive advertisements and inducements to entice foreign nationals to travel to the United States for the purpose of giving birth on American soil," the order says.

WATCH: How the birthright citizenship decision impacts Trump's immigration agenda

"They promise citizenship; access to public benefits; and short-term stays in specialized facilities, hotels, or rentals, but often fail to deliver on these promises. These operators coach their clients to misrepresent the purpose and duration of their travel to consular and border officials to obtain visas authorizing entry into the United States."

The Republican Party has embraced the mission. In late July, the office of the attorney general in Texas announced a "sweeping investigation" into potentially unlawful birth tourism schemes after some south Texas hospitals advertised birthing services in Mexico.

Legal challenges expected

Asked Thursday how his orders would survive Supreme Court scrutiny when his last attempt failed, Trump deferred to White House staff secretary Will Scharf, who, like his boss, sounded alarms about "birth tourism." He emphasized consular discretion to grant visas.

"What we're doing is taking legally validated means that are clearly within our disposal and targeting them to this birth tourism industry. There's absolutely nothing here that runs afoul of any of the Supreme Court rulings on the subject," Sharf said.

Advocates against the proposed changes said they believe the constitutional amendment and Supreme Court decisions will again stop the administration's efforts to restrict birthright citizenship.

"The bottom line is that the Supreme Court already considered the Trump administration's plea to rewrite the Constitution and rejected it," said Cody Wofsy, deputy director at the American Civil Liberties Union Immigrants' Rights Project.

"Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the 14th Amendment, and no amount of executive orders is going to change that."

Associated Press writer Melissa Goldin contributed.

title: ICE and Data Centers Aren't New, But Face Growing Pushback as They Intertwine | Truthout
authors: Loretta Graceffo, Austin C. McCoy, Jon Letman, Kelly Hayes, Derek Seidman, Amy Goodman, Chris Walker, Victoria Valenzuela, Ariana Figueroa, Amy Green

This prison, like some of the AI data centers, also threatens ecosystems and several endangered species in the Everglades.
This battle against AI data centers is also about how local communities should invest public resources.

text:
On July 13, residents of Neptune Township, New Jersey, voted to ban AI data centers and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) jails from being built in their town. While protests against the construction of AI data centers and ICE facilities have increased since Donald Trump’s reelection, the Neptune Township ordinance is the first in the U.S. reflecting a connection between the deportation regime and Big Tech.

Neptune residents’ move to oppose technofascism in their town also demonstrates the potential to form new coalitions, powered by grassroots organizing, for more democratic participation in local development. Ben Dziobek, executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network (CRAN), a New Jersey-based organization that helped mobilize support for the bans, told Insider NJ, “Banning ICE detention centers is the same fight as banning data centers … Neptune is deciding what it wants built in its town and what it doesn’t.”

Of course, the current upsurge in demonstrations against AI data centers and ICE immigrant jails is not in response to new phenomena. On the one hand, tech companies like Amazon and Microsoft have been building data centers for years, mostly to warehouse large amounts of data that governments, corporations, and consumers use for digital storage. However, the construction and operation of these new AI data centers raise questions about the undemocratic nature of economic development and Big Tech. Elon Musk’s xAI bypassed federal environmental regulations to build gas turbines for its Tennessee facilities. Meta worked covertly with some of Louisiana’s state elected officials to plan and build AI centers. And Trump, in his second term, has sought to restrict local and state regulation of AI, further greasing the skids for construction. These data centers pose environmental, health, and economic threats to residents and workers. They are linked to noise pollution and exorbitant levels of water and electric usage — and residents have complained of increases in utility bills.

On the other hand, ICE has relied on a network of hundreds of facilities since its formation in 2003. According to a 2024 Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse report on immigration, ICE held nearly 40,000 adults at the end of Joe Biden’s presidential term in January 2025. The Trump administration has sought to dramatically escalate ICE arrests and detentions to enact its white nationalist immigration agenda.

This craven drive to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible is fueling this administration’s attempts to expand its network of camps, including by converting closed prisons and warehouses into ICE facilities. Florida’s infamous South Florida Detention Center, also known as “Alligator Alcatraz,” is one of the most prominent examples of a swiftly built detention camp enacting this administration’s cruel immigration policy. People detained there complained of the inhumane conditions in which they were held, saying that they faced overflowing toilets and were denied prescribed medication and adequate food.

This prison, like some of the AI data centers, also threatens ecosystems and several endangered species in the Everglades. The construction of the South Florida Detention Center generated protests from Floridians and others opposing the construction of the facility and the conditions inside. In fact, protesters gathered for “Freedom Vigils” outside of “Alligator Alcatraz” every Sunday since August 2025. The political and legal pressure from protesters, people being detained, environmental and civil rights groups, and elected officials forced its closure in June 2026.

The movement to stop data centers and detention camps during Trump’s second term has been relatively successful. Between March and June 2025, protests helped delay or stop 20 data center projects, Kristin Toussaint from Fast Company reports. Opposition to AI data centers continues to stymie Big Tech in 2026. Between January and March of this year, people across the U.S., from Arizona to Virginia, have obstructed or blocked more than $130 billion in data center development.

On the surface, the fight against data centers and detention camps might seem unrelated. However, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) touts its use of AI in immigration enforcementon its website. Tech companies have forged relationships with DHS and ICE to assist in immigration enforcement. Spotify, to much outrage from listeners, ran recruitment advertisements for ICE. The federal government awarded Palantir a $30 million contract last year to develop an “ImmigrationOS” surveillance platform to track people suspected to be undocumented. Palantir’s Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement (“ELITE”) app tracks and maps people targeted by ICE. And surely, immigrants are not the only people that ICE targets using these apps, as one Minneapolis activist suspected that ICE used these apps to surveil them as well. New data centers would surely help support DHS and ICE’s use of AI in immigration enforcement and the squashing of dissent. And, if DHS’s and ICE’s uses of AI are not enough, former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons articulated a sinister aspiration for the expansion of the U.S.’s deportation machine through neoliberal and technofacist rhetoric. Lyons said at the Border Security Expo in Phoenix in 2025 that the U.S. needed “to get better at treating this [deportation] like a business.” The country needs to build a system that operates “like [Amazon] Prime, but with human beings,” he added.

This relationship between tech companies and federal and state governments in constructing and fortifying immigration enforcement highlights further threats to rights of Americans, undocumented people, and to nature. CRAN demonstrates their understanding of this relationship on its website. The organization points to Palantir Chair Peter Thiel’s disdain for democracy and billionaire Larry Ellison’s musings about using AI to police everyone to illustrate how Big Tech seeks to use generative artificial intelligence to plunder communities of resources, accumulate capital, consolidate political power, surveil people, and conduct destructive wars. This presidential administration has proven that it is a willing partner in this endeavor.

Neptune residents’ and the Climate Revolution Action Network’s fight against data centers and detention camps underscores how the struggle for democracy extends beyond voting in elections every two and four years. This battle against AI data centers is also about how local communities should invest public resources. As organizers Astra Taylor and Saul Levin stated about the data center opposition: “It’s about who controls the economy and whether regular people have a say in the decisions that affect them.” Neptune’s refusal to build these centers and CRAN’s statewide struggle to ban data centers in New Jersey contribute another model for fighting undemocratic AI data centers and ICE facilities and to assert a more humane vision for development.

Few people should want to live in the shadow of energy-sucking and noisy AI data centers with their neighbors living in fear of ICE kidnapping. This sentiment about economic development applies to policing, immigration, and citizenship. The communities that are opposing ICE detention camps are refusing complicity in this administration’s deportation regime. And many opponents of these detention centers are demanding a more expansive understanding of citizenship that might not include an undocumented person’s ability to vote in elections, but a community life that supports their human rights as workers and residents. It is time that all of us see these struggles as linked and as part of a larger vision that rejects undemocratic development and tech-fueled policing.

text:
Since humanity has been grappling with a myriad of contentious conflicts across the world, one of their core repercussions has been mass displacement and immigration. A highly devastating phenomenon for war-torn lives, inflicted by the heinous desires of some leaders, the sheer number of forcibly displaced people last year, 2025, was 117.8 million, roughly one in every 70 people on Earth. actually It is an unequivocal reality since the formation of communities on the face of the planet, not a new issue, but nowadays its brooding over our minds, as the political weaponization of the migration and its policies has been dominating the mainstream social interests, it has transformed into such an extent, that can even determine the direction of transnational relations and national politics, it is apparent from its rousing consolidation since the end of the cold war, So the question remains: Has immigration become the most potent political weapon in contemporary geopolitics? And more, it ought to be addressed.

The Global Migration Crisis

To begin with, immigration crisis is a real-world issue, yet not a isolated episode, but a certain ubiquitous operation spanned throughout the presence of the nationalities, however, in today’s world it is more complex, to stay with that, almost 41.6 million refugees is living under this fragile label, driven out from own residence and soil, as per reports, war in Sudan generated 2.8 million refugees and 10.5 million internally displaced, and the cases in Ukrain, syria, DRC(Democratic Republic of the Congo ), Palestine, etc.. does not numerically differ from it, just piles up the stakes of amount. The structural apprehension of real-world events would direct us to the triggering drivers of it; according to the World Bank, they attributed it to devastating inhumane conflicts, widening income disparities, demographic pressures, and shifting weather patterns. Under those circumstances, the amount of migration growth has already escalated briskly; over the span of time, the sum would only upsurge to the pinnacle. Correspondingly, a closer gaze into the issues would persuade you that most of the causes are driven by human deeds themselves, particularly the stringent political deterioration that exacerbates the problem.

The Humanitarian Toll of Forced Migration

To put it differently, Since 2014, the IOM’s(International Organization for Migration) Missing Migrants Project has recorded 81,912 migrant deaths worldwide; 46,775 of these were caused by drowning, and the Central Mediterranean route alone accounted for 26,474 deaths, navigates the miserable condition that immigrants are going through, at the same time the fact of that 38% of displaced people are children (45 million) has shed light on the overt failure of major developments that some of the world organizations boasting of; likewise per year 305,000 children are born as refugees around the world, unsurprisingly 7 in 10 refugees live in protracted or permanent displacement due to generational condition highlighting the severity of the human predicament to resist this.

The Political Weaponization of Migration

Moving swiftly to the systematic weaponization of immigration would utterly swerve our reckoning from the prevailing framework. As per stats 68% of refugees are hosted by low middle income countries, not by the wealthy nations, here the irony is, if the poorest countries endure the burden, why does immigration staying as a flashpoint of politics in wealthy countries, for past years migration issues imparted ardent political agenda in election campaigns, politicians and leaders emboldening on to sticking them on the crest of the their manifestos, consequently, it endowed paramount developments in favor of them, still the question of “how they weaponized it” does require a crystal understanding.

The incident of former american president bill clinton’s unbrazen mentioning of migrants as “illegal aliens” irrespective of their intentions have already exposed the penchant of leaders to it, in fact political candidates usually tend to run on making immigration reforms, But when elections settle down they literally don’t accomplish it, rather merely approach it as a political issue than a policy issue, patently neglecting the pragmatic approach of the issue, it is quite obvious when the practices and policies on this has been ineffective in bringing down the numbers of immigrants for a long time, by all means keeping immigration contracts high on political agenda it is something that can be exploited in all different ways, the sweeping campaign of Donald J. Trump in last presidential election has gently reflected on his unwavering push for immigration policies by demonizing the immigrants from Mexico, global South countries, etc. In 2021, around 6,000 migrants from Morocco, with the administration’s acknowledgement, entered Ceuta, a Spanish enclave city, illegally. In response, an extensive uproar has broken out in the streets of Spain. Morocco was aware that immigration is a pivotal political issue there; in this case, Buffer States across the world see immigration as a threat, but in larger countries they exploit the same threat. In 2010, Muammar Gaddafi put forward a Warning that he would allow large immigration from sub-Saharan countries to Europe through Libya unless Europe pays five billion per year.

Borders, Security, and the New Politics of Migration

In addition to that, apart from the Geopolitical threat it has been orchestrated as a rhetoric in some terrain, particularly, in the persuasion of building strong border enforcement governments spent billions, for instance in 2021 alone USA spent 1.9 billion on US border patrol in Mexican borders, likewise coast guard agency frontex has spent 922 million on EU border, in tandem with that, when the cold war ends there was just 15 nation-state borders, but three decades later it has exponentially increased into 70. To mention that, this market is worth tens of billions worldwide; this industry grows rapidly in the West, even though the West isn’t at the top of most sheltering sides for the forcibly displaced. According to statistics, Iran and Turkey reside at the top of the list for the most sheltering countries for forcibly displaced Folks. This brings the political maneuvering of Europe into the light.

Immigration became a major political concern in Europe following the 1990s, since the outpouring of migration, mainstream media were bound to cover conflict-based and negative tidings only, which has spiked public questions. Subsequently, it turned out to be politically significant; politicians prompted voters to support the anti-immigration parties. In response to that, parties adopted stricter immigration policies to compete. That is why, in the public sphere, anti-immigration parties influence policies beyond immigration vulnerabilities; it has the potential to change the public attitude, election outcomes, and government policies to a greater extent. From the unravelling realities around us, from the ranting political campaigns to lethal refugee transportation, it indicates the obscure facets of immigration policies.

text:
The Glenwood Springs City Council voted 6-1 on Thursday to pursue legal action against the owner of the Midland Avenue property housing a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility, seeking to stop the building from being used to temporarily hold or detain people.

The council directed City Attorney Karl Hanlon to prepare legal enforcement action, sanctions and injunctive relief against JG Housing Solutions LLC, the owner of the property at 100 Midland Ave., including units 110 and 210, for alleged zoning and land use code violations. The city plans to initially pursue the case in state court rather than directly suing ICE or the U.S. General Services Administration.

JG Housing Solutions LLC did not respond to a request for comment from the Post Independent.

Councilor Ray Schmahl was the only council member to vote against the motion.

The decision comes after the city confirmed ICE continued using the property as a temporary hold facility after the Glenwood Springs Planning and Zoning Commission revoked its special use permit earlier this year.

Emergency medical personnel responded to the facility on July 24 for a medical call, and information from that response confirmed people were being held there, Hanlon said.

“That, in my mind, gave me the factual basis to say that it is a ripe claim to potentially bring back to you for action on the zoning violation,” Hanlon said.

He said the July 24 response gave the city evidence it could use in court to show the property was still being used in a way no longer permitted under city zoning.

The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-1 on April 28 to revoke a special use permit issued in 2003 that allowed ICE to operate a temporary hold facility at the property.

The permit limited holds to 12 hours. The commission revoked it after reviewing evidence showing people had been held beyond that limit on multiple occasions.

Neither ICE, the property owner nor the General Services Administration appealed the decision, which became final around on June 4. Under the city’s current zoning code, a temporary hold or detention facility is not a permitted use at the property.

The topic drew a large crowd on Thursday, filling the City Council chambers and a second room inside Town Hall used for overflow seating. Many of those in attendance urged the council to enforce the Planning and Zoning Commission’s decision and take action against the property owner.

The revocation does not prevent ICE from continuing to use the property for other purposes allowed under the zoning code, including office or staging space.

Instead, the city would seek preliminary and permanent injunctions preventing the property owner from allowing the site to be used to hold or detain people.

Hanlon recommended going after the property owner rather than directly naming ICE or the General Services Administration because he said that gives the city its best chance of keeping the case in state court.

Even there, he warned the city faces a difficult legal fight.

Asked to estimate the city’s chances of obtaining an injunction, he said they were probably less than 25%.

The main issue would likely be the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution. The property owner could argue that local zoning enforcement interferes with a core function of the federal government.

Hanlon said the city would argue that prohibiting ICE from holding people at the Glenwood Springs location would not stop the agency from enforcing immigration law.

“If I were the federal government, I would argue that it is immigration enforcement writ large that is the core function that we are impeding,” Hanlon said. “I think my position would be you don’t use the facility that much. You have lots of other opportunities, and nobody is saying you can’t enforce. We’re saying you can’t violate our zoning code by holding people there.”

The potential cost of the case also became a major part of the council’s discussion.

Hanlon estimated the city could spend about $50,000 to reach a preliminary injunction hearing or get through an initial motion to dismiss in state court. A state court case taken through trial could cost between $250,000 and $300,000 and take 18 to 24 months.

A federal case could cost about $100,000 in its early stages and roughly $500,000 through trial, with a trial potentially three years away.

If the city does not obtain a preliminary injunction, the property could continue being used as a hold facility while the case moves forward.

Hanlon also said opposing attorneys could seek sanctions under Rule 11 if they argue the city’s lawsuit is frivolous or groundless. Another law firm has reviewed the issue, and Hanlon said the city believes it has a good-faith basis to bring the case.

Council members generally agreed the city should enforce its land use code but raised concerns about how much money and time should be spent on the case.

Schmahl, who voted against the motion, focused on the financial risk.

“I find my definition of courageous local leadership to be not wasting the taxpayers’ money,” Schmahl said. “I’ve been told over and over again that this is a waste of money.”

Councilor David Townsley also raised concerns about the cost of a long legal battle but said the city should not set a precedent of ignoring violations of its land use code.

Mayor Pro Tem Erin Zalinski said the city had heard months of frustration from residents who believed officials were not acting quickly enough but said the city needed evidence it could defend in court before taking action.

“We had to wait until we had something that was tangible and actionable and defensible,” Zalinski said.

Public commenters overwhelmingly urged the city to move forward with enforcement. Several specifically encouraged the council to pursue the private property owner in state court rather than directly suing federal agencies.

Glenwood Springs resident Ashley Stahl made that argument during public comment.

“Don’t take this to federal court,” Stahl said. “Don’t name GSA and ICE. The violation in front of you is simple. A private landlord is leasing space for a use our code simply does not permit.”

Hanlon said the city could also pursue a separate municipal court case over the July 24 violation, where city code allows fines of up to $1,000 per day. However, proving continuing daily violations would require the city to show when people were actually being held inside the facility.

He said seeking an injunction in state court offers a more direct path toward stopping the use altogether.

title: Commentary: Immigrant kids deserve to keep their lawyers | Opinion | yakimaherald.com
description:
The Trump administration has jettisoned the way thousands of immigrant children receive legal help.
On Friday, the Department of Health and Human Services ended the contract with the Acacia Center for Justice after nearly two decades, leaving more than 20,000 unaccompanied kids in legal limbo.
The Acacia Center for Justice was contracted by ORR to coordinate representation through a vast network of providers — lawyers, advocates, faith leaders and social workers.

Abandoned and powerless children are not the “worst of the worst.” They deserve nurturing and compassion, not hate.
text:
The Trump administration has jettisoned the way thousands of immigrant children receive legal help. On Friday, the Department of Health and Human Services ended the contract with the Acacia Center for Justice after nearly two decades, leaving more than 20,000 unaccompanied kids in legal limbo.

Federal officials claim it’s a contract dispute. That’s a convenient excuse for their moral failure.

Federal immigration data shows that many of these children came to this country seeking refuge from harm. Some have been tortured and trafficked. Others were separated from their parents at the border. Most seek asylum, and many just want to be reunited with their families.

Congress recognized such trauma in 2008 when it passed the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, which requires the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) to provide legal representation for children navigating the immigration process. The Acacia Center for Justice was contracted by ORR to coordinate representation through a vast network of providers — lawyers, advocates, faith leaders and social workers.

But now this network clashes with what White House border czar Tom Homan calls its “deportation-maxxing” agenda. Although he promises to focus on arresting the “worst of the worst,” Homan’s strategy also involves targeting legal protections for vulnerable children so that the administration can accelerate their removal.

Administration officials have consistently defended child deportations by saying that “Children deserve to be with their parents.” They seem blind to the irony — that the Trump administration’s mass detention and deportation policies have separated more than 205,000 children from their parents as of May of this year, forcing thousands into detention or foster care.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard told me the agency “remains fully compliant with its legal and regulatory obligations” under the 2008 law.

But since November, its actions have defied that claim. HHS has refused to pay $65 million in overdue legal fees owed to the Acacia Center and its network of providers.

HHS says it’s withholding the money because the Acacia Center won’t turn over confidential information about its clients, including unredacted medical evaluations and details about their immigration cases. The center’s lawyers say that those demands force them to violate their attorney-client privilege and that the information has never been sought by any previous presidential administration — including during President Donald Trump’s first term.

HHS is also accusing the Acacia Center of fraud. Despite repeated questioning, however, HHS has provided no evidence to prove those fraud claims and, notably, makes the allegations exclusively in public statements, not in legal documents.

It’s all a smokescreen for the callous and calculated tactics HHS is employing. Since last September, the Department of Homeland Security has tried to coerce unaccompanied minor children to self-deport by telling them they could either give up their asylum claims and leave the country or face long-term detention. Many of these children have survived violence, separation and dangerous journeys. Thousands of Guatemalan children have come from persecuted Indigenous communities and were targeted for deportation until lawyers intervened.

Immigration advocates say the goal of ending the contract is to slowly destroy the program by grinding down the financial health of the nonprofit organizations providing the children’s safety net.

By withholding payment for services already provided, HHS has forced at least 40 law firms and service providers to lay off staff, withhold services and leave children without representation, said Bettina Rodriguez-Schlege, chief of staff of the Acacia Center, at a news conference Friday.

The impact on the kids may be profound. Prolonged uncertainty “can really deepen anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, with consequences that extend well into adulthood,” Dr. C. Nicholas Cuneo, an assistant professor of Pediatrics and Medicine at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine who works with refugees, told reporters on Friday.

But a trusted attorney “can buffer that harm,” he added, by helping children understand an incomprehensible process, giving them a safe and stable environment, and connecting them with health care, schools, housing and other support.

Research also shows that when children go to court without an attorney, there’s a high likelihood they will lose their asylum claims and be deported back to the countries they fled.

Erin Maxwell, co-director of the Detained Immigrant Children’s Project, described how children who have been detained for months in crowded detention centers are wearing down and choosing “to return to extremely unsafe situations in their countries of origin because of detention fatigue.”

Money is not the problem here. Congress has set aside money for the legal representation of unaccompanied minors, although it’s never been enough to meet the need. And the Trump administration has repeatedly shown it can find the money when the president wants to spend it. The $65 million in services rendered owed to the Acacia Center is far less than the $101 million in federal money spent on “beautification projects” to prepare Washington for the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration and the $600 million spent on a new White House ballroom.

By Monday, one of the Acacia Center’s partners, the International Rescue Committee, announced it would continue to represent unaccompanied children in immigration court despite the loss of funding. That’s promising, but it’s not sustainable.

Americans should be asking ourselves if we’re willing to scar a generation of young people so that this administration can pursue its anti-immigrant policies. Abandoned and powerless children are not the “worst of the worst.” They deserve nurturing and compassion, not hate.

title: The Leadership Conference Condemns Senate Confirmation of Todd Blanche as Attorney General
description:
Blanche turned the Department’s investigative power against civil rights organizations and the people who shine a light on extremism and hate crimes, which have claimed too many of our family members, friends, and neighbors.
Todd Blanche is a man wholly undeserving and unfit to serve as the Attorney General of the United States.
Millions of Americans depend on the Justice Department carrying out its mission, and we will carry the consequences when the individual who leads it acts as the president’s personal lawyer instead of the people’s attorney.
Congress retains the power to conduct oversight, to control appropriations, and to raise questions about an officer who abuses public trust.
We will watch and document what this Attorney General does with that authority and be ready to continue to fight for our civil rights and equal justice under the law.” ###
text:
A PDF copy of this statement can be found here.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Maya Wiley, president and CEO of The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, released the following statement after the Senate voted 50-49 to confirm Todd Blanche as Attorney General of the United States:

“Today, the Senate handed the Justice Department to a man who does not believe it belongs to the American people, and he spent two years proving it. Congress built that Department in 1870 to secure the rights of newly freed people, and neither that mission nor the Civil Rights Division survives a leader who treats the law as a tool for protecting one man and punishing his critics. A majority of the Senate decided it could live with that.

Blanche’s record is clear. Just some of his abuses include firing Erez Reuveni, the career lawyer who told a federal judge the truth about the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, knowing full well the personal consequences he may face. Blanche turned the Department’s investigative power against civil rights organizations and the people who shine a light on extremism and hate crimes, which have claimed too many of our family members, friends, and neighbors. Blanche signed a memo trying to permanently bar the government from pursuing claims against the president and his family, shielding them, yet refusing everyday people justice. He is still finding ways to give taxpayer money to people who attacked this country. He has stated his intention to end all access to reproductive healthcare and to interfere with state law. He left survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking, like Dani Bensky, waiting for answers he never intended to give, while failing to prosecute claims or take responsibility for re-traumatizing them with incompetent and unlawful disclosures of their personal information and images.

The warnings came from people with no partisan stake in the outcome: a large and diverse coalition of non-partisan, non-profit organizations, more than 1,200 former Justice Department employees, the New York City Bar Association, 101 former judges, and Epstein survivors who described what his misconduct cost them.

Todd Blanche is a man wholly undeserving and unfit to serve as the Attorney General of the United States.

And still, the senators who cast the deciding votes to confirm Blanche decided to accept his empty promises rather than stand up for equal justice on behalf of their constituents. Doubt expressed in a hallway and abandoned on the floor is not oversight. It’s a performance.

The Department Blanche now runs is supposed to ensure every voter can cast a ballot for leaders who are accountable to us, makes sure we all have equal opportunity at work and school, or could decide whether armed federal immigration agents can harass voters at polling places. Millions of Americans depend on the Justice Department carrying out its mission, and we will carry the consequences when the individual who leads it acts as the president’s personal lawyer instead of the people’s attorney.

A confirmation does not end our fight to protect our communities. Congress retains the power to conduct oversight, to control appropriations, and to raise questions about an officer who abuses public trust. We will be urging them to use that power. We will watch and document what this Attorney General does with that authority and be ready to continue to fight for our civil rights and equal justice under the law.”

text:
APPLETON — Community organizers and residents gathered Thursday in Appleton to protest the reopening of the Prairie Correctional Facility as a detention center for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

More than two dozen demonstrators were at the Flags of Honor Memorial holding signs of opposition. One house across the street from the memorial displayed Trump 2020 campaign signs as well as signs expressing support for ICE.

A demonstrator in a pickle costume with a bullhorn exchanged verbal jabs with those who stood at the house while another man revved a small engine on a dirt bike to drown out any message over the bullhorn.

The short and sometimes sophomoric exchanges showed just how raw and emotional people feel about the reopening of the Appleton prison.

Longtime prison owner CoreCivic announced Tuesday that the company had agreed to a five-year contract with ICE, with detainees expected to arrive in Appleton in the fourth quarter of 2026 and full ramp-up in the second quarter of 2027.

A day later, CoreCivic announced that it had sold the facility to the Department of Homeland Security for nearly $500 million but still expected to be managing it as an ICE detention center.

The 1,600-bed facility could hold more people within its walls than the entire population in Appleton by mid-2027. The Swift County website lists the city’s population at 1,411.

Nicole Meyer, an organizer of the protest, attempted to give out some baked goods and pamphlets to the people across the street from the demonstration Thursday, hoping to explain why there is opposition to the reopening. Shortly after she approached the curb, however, the group there realized she was part of the protest. They immediately told her she was trespassing and she left as asked.

The opposing groups otherwise stayed on their respective sides of the street. An Appleton police squad car was present for the entire protest from 5 to 6:30 p.m. A Swift County Sheriff’s Office squad vehicle was present for part of the time.

The West Central Tribune observed one pickup truck with an American flag, a sign stating “Welcome ICE” and another sign on its tailgate stating that Democrats should also be deported. It was parked across the street before it began circling the demonstration area a handful of times.

Meyer told the West Central Tribune that she worked at the prison before it closed in 2010.

“You have to remember these (were) inmates that were convicted of a crime and sentenced,” she said. “They were treated fairly and we had a lot of oversight.”

Meyer said she opposes the reopening of the prison not only because its purpose is “locking people up for being a stranger,” but that she also fears ICE and the Department of Homeland Security will have none of the same oversight that she experienced while working there.

“In the contract it says local police are not allowed on the property unless invited,” she said. “There’s no transparency. It’s just different,” she said, mentioning the numerous reports of alleged violations at other various ICE detention facilities across the nation. “There are a lot of human rights violations. They’re violating constitutional rights and nobody is policing them.”

She also added that the people who would be detained at the Prairie Correctional Facility wouldn’t necessarily be convicted of any crime.

“The rapists and murderers are already locked up,” she said. “These are not people who are committing crimes. These are people who are here on asylum. These are people who are here on work visas. These are people who follow family here, that work here, and are just trying to make a living. And we’re spending all our federal tax dollars on locking them up instead of letting them add to our economy. It doesn’t make any sense to me.”

Meyer, who is from the Appleton area, said any economic benefit to the community would be temporary if it exists at all.

“You’re gonna run out of people to deport, unless they’re planning on filling it up with somebody else,” she said. “If the policy is mass deportation, why are we opening up more detention centers?”

Tom Nelson, another Appleton area resident at the protest, said the reopening of the prison did not come as a surprise.

“To be honest it’s a double-edged sword,” he said. “This is one of the most economically depressed areas in the state. ... There’s just such a shortage of good paying jobs out here,” he said.

“We got a facility out there that could put a lot of people to work, but man, the fact it’s gonna be housing ICE detainees,” he said as he shook his head. Nelson said he believes most people in Appleton feel as conflicted as he does.

Nelson has driven people who were fearful of being detained.

“I can’t tell you how many times I’ve had to circle parking lots and pick up people at alternative locations just because they were afraid that either they or their spouse or their kid were gonna get picked up by ICE.”

He said hearing firsthand accounts from immigrants are why he came to the protest Thursday.

“People see what’s in the headlines, but they don’t see the impact or think about the impact this has on individuals,” he said.

The Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota, a nonprofit organization that provides free legal representation to low-income immigrants and refugees in Minnesota and North Dakota, published a statement Wednesday noting the large size of the facility and the remote location with few legal resources.

“It’s a staggering increase over the immigration detention capacity currently contracted to county jails,” the organization said.

“ ... Appleton sits roughly 150 miles west of the Twin Cities, where the majority of Minnesota's immigration attorneys, accredited representatives and interpreters are based. Detention far from counsel is a functional obstacle to due process.”

Minnesota Sen. Torrey Westrom, R-Alexandria, applauded the reopening of the prison in a statement issued Tuesday, calling it “welcome news for Senate District 12” and the rest of west central Minnesota.

“Bringing it back into service will create approximately 450 new jobs and provide a significant economic boost,” his statement reads. He remained enthusiastic after the sale was announced, calling it “all good news for Appleton!” in a Facebook post.

text:
A Reno-area activist group plans to protest an aviation company over its reported work with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement to transport detainees.

"Our goal is to de-ICE the Reno airport,” said Deborah Achtenberg of the Biggest Little Action Group.

The Reno-Tahoe Airport Authority confirmed recently that ICE has been engaging in immigration enforcement actions at the airport.

The protest is planned from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. Friday, Aug. 14, at Stellar Aviation, which provides private flight services from a hangar connected to Reno-Tahoe International Airport.

“How many people realize that every Friday morning, some of their neighbors — generally hardworking, law-abiding people — are put in shackles and flown, against their will, from the Stellar Aviation portion of the Reno airport to parts unknown?” Achtenberg told the Reno Gazette Journal. “We want to bring attention to the unsafe, cruel and inhumane situation ICE flight passengers are in here in Northern Nevada."

Stellar’s customer service manager said the business was aware of the planned protest next week and would have no comment.

“We already have law enforcement and legal teams in place for this, so unfortunately no statements will be made,” she said.

Reno-Tahoe Airport Authority spokesperson Jena Esposito said its police department is aware of potential protest activity near Stellar Aviation.

"We are in close communication with our local law enforcement partners and are monitoring the situation," she said. "As always, the safety and security of passengers, employees, tenants and all who use our facilities remains our top priority."

The Biggest Little Action Group has an online RSVP form set up in order to gauge attendance. It describes the event as “a nonviolent standout.”

Attendees are asked to meet at the intersection of Rock and Mill on the public sidewalk outside Stellar Aviation and to not park in Stellar’s lot.

The action comes as ICE expands its enforcement actions at airports to target travelers at check-in counters and gates who have overstayed visas, sometimes for years. Immigration attorneys told ABC News that some people swept up in the airport enforcement effort have valid work authorization and no criminal history.

title: U.S. citizen claims wrongful detention during ICE operation in Norfolk | WAVY.com
description:
Video obtained by 10 On Your Side shows the confrontation with Brittany Ramirez Corona and federal agents.
Brittany Ramirez Corona said agents handcuffed her and took her to the federal building in downtown Norfolk.
“I was just like, every time I kept saying I’m a U.S. citizen,” Ramirez Corona said.

text:
NORFOLK, Va. (WAVY) — An 18-year-old Norfolk woman says she was detained by federal immigration agents Friday morning after arriving at the scene of an immigration enforcement operation involving her husband, even after she told agents she was a U.S. citizen.

Brittany Ramirez Corona said she was detained along Tidewater Drive after receiving a call that her husband and several workers had been taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

By the time she arrived, her husband was gone, but his vehicle was still there. Brittany Ramirez Corona said she went to retrieve the vehicle but was confronted by agents.

Video obtained by 10 On Your Side shows the confrontation with Brittany Ramirez Corona and federal agents. In the video, she can be heard telling agents the vehicle belonged to her husband and asking them to let her go, and that she initially did not provide identification.

Brittany Ramirez Corona said agents handcuffed her and took her to the federal building in downtown Norfolk. She said she showed them her identification and Social Security information, but that agents questioned the identification, calling it fake.

“I was just like, every time I kept saying I’m a U.S. citizen,” Ramirez Corona said. “How is this fake?”

She said agents fingerprinted her and still could not verify her citizenship.

Ramirez Corona was released from federal custody Friday morning. She emerged from the building with visible bruising around her wrists, which she attributed to the handcuffs.

Ramirez Corona also said she was with her 4-year-old sister when she was detained.

Her 15-year-old sister, Julie Ramirez Corona, said she came to the scene to pick up the younger child and brought Brittany’s birth certificate, which she said showed Brittany was born in Norfolk.

Julie Ramirez Corona explained that agents placed her and the 4-year-old sister in the back of an ICE vehicle, later dropping them off at a nearby Harris Teeter. Julie Ramirez Corona then made her way to the federal building.

She said she initially had difficulty getting into the federal building because she was a minor and only had a school identification card. She said agents did not immediately accept the birth certificate as proof of Brittany Ramirez Corona’s citizenship.

“They take innocent people,” Julie Ramirez Corona said. “They’re taking them to these facilities. God knows where.”

As word spread that a woman who said she was a U.S. citizen had been detained, demonstrators gathered outside the federal building calling for her release.

Carmel Saucer, a naturalized U.S. citizen who joined the demonstration, said she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the detention.

“As a naturalized citizen myself, I just feel so strongly about what is happening and how the rule of law just seemingly doesn’t matter,” Saucer said.

Ramirez Corona said she plans to take legal action over her detention.

Her husband, Osman Amaya, remained in ICE custody as of Friday afternoon, according to Brittany Ramirez Corona.

10 On Your Side reached out to ICE for information about Brittany Ramirez Corona’s detention, including why she was taken into custody and whether agents were aware of her claim of U.S. citizenship at the time of her arrest. The agency had not responded as of Friday afternoon.

text:
A week after the release of the highly anticipated "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," the White House made an Instagram post that isn't settling right with Marvel fans.

On Aug. 6, the official White House Instagram page made a post about ICE agents, using Spider-Man imagery. The 4-photo carousel begins with a photo of Spider-Man releasing his iconic web, with the last photo showing several men handcuffed and covered in spiderwebs, overlooked by an ICE agent.

"Your friendly neighborhood ICE agents," the post reads.

The Instagram post quickly gained traction, with more than 32,000 users leaving comments, as of Aug. 7.

"Spider-Man would not support this," one user said on the post. Another commented: "My spider senses are tingling for a lawsuit."

"Like spiderman, our law enforcement officers keeping our homeland safe are all heroes. Leftists triggered by the use of a fictional character to generate viral conversation with the American people need to look in the mirror and ask themselves if Spider-Man would endorse the crimes committed by these dangerous criminal illegal aliens that the Trump administration is working to remove from our communities," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told USA TODAY in an emailed statement on Aug. 7.

Falling in line with several other recent posts made by the White House recently, the "Spider-Man" post appears to be AI-generated. When the fourth photo of the carousel was uploaded into AI-image detectors Sightengine, Zero GPT and Deep AI, the image tested between 96-99% likely to be AI-generated.

Walt Disney Co., which owns the Marvel franchise, did not immediately responded when contacted by USA TODAY on Aug. 7.

Not the first

Earlier in the week, the White House received backlash for releasing what appeared to be an AI-generated video parodying Nicole Kidman's advert for AMC Theatres. Parodying AMC's "We Make Movies Better" ad, the White House's video showed a man wearing a Make America Great Again ballcap walking through the halls of the White House.

text:
The format for the town hall meeting held by the Adams County Health Department, over Zoom, was dry. The questions, posted in a chat, were urgent.

How long would it take for TB to kill someone? Last year there were rumors of TB, why did you guys take a long time to ask for an investigation? Do you have any evidence that staff or employees of the facility have TB?

The Adams County Health Department held a community briefing and town hall on Friday about the now nearly two month-long stalemate over at least one case of tuberculosis at the GEO Aurora ICE Processing Center.

More than 50 people, including health department staff, joined the call. Some questions at the town hall came in anonymously, others were from immigrant-rights advocates or reporters.

The answers, provided by two top county health officials, plus the state epidemiologist, underscored how little they know about what’s happening inside.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which oversees federal detention facilities, and GEO Group, the private, publicly traded corporation that runs the one in Aurora, have thwarted any local public health investigation since June.

ICE has said the person with TB was moved and there's no longer active TB there, but it's not allowed a public health investigation, as required by state law.

Questions and some answers

When an anonymous audience member asked how long it would take for TB to kill someone, a deep concern advocates have expressed, Dr. Wendy Bamberg, the county's chief medical officer, explained that it’s complicated.

“It's not common, but we do see deaths from tuberculosis. But generally we're talking about months to years,” she said.

TB is a serious, contagious but curable lung disease, treatable via a long-term regimen of antibiotics. But it can be fatal if untreated.

Bamberg said it is a slow infection, but depends on the person. Someone under five, living with HIV or who is severely immunocompromised, might be at an increased risk to progression to active TB from an initial infection.

About 10% of people progress from latent TB to active tuberculosis infection; about half are within the first year or two. “Hopefully we see no deaths from tuberculosis,” she said.

Prominent immigrant rights advocate Jeanette Vizguerra asked about rumors of TB in the facility last year and why it took public health a long time to ask for an investigation.

“The Adams County Health Department has received some vague reports of illness over time in the facility, whether that be gastrointestinal illness or respiratory illness. We have not seen any other laboratory-confirmed cases of TB,” said Kelly Weidenbach, the agency’s executive director.

She said the last time it had a confirmed TB case in the facility was September 2024.

When its communicable disease epidemiology team launched an investigation into GI and respiratory illnesses in January, she said. Adams county issued a public health order requesting additional information from GEO and ICE.

“There was not compliance,” she said, noting the agency didn’t have a laboratory report, a clinician diagnosis or any other information to rely on. “There was not adequate information that we had to really pursue this from an enforcement standpoint earlier this year.”

When asked if any GEO Aurora facility staff have TB, Bamberg said public health authorities do not have knowledge of more than the single case of TB associated with the facility.

“Currently we don't have information to know if there are other cases of tuberculosis at the facility other than the same reports that you all are seeing,” she said.

State health department joins the conversation

Dr. Rachel Herlihy, the state’s epidemiologist, joined the call as well and answered questions, marking the first time someone from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has made public comments on the situation, beyond issuing press releases.

“I'll say that this is a uniquely frustrating experience and a uniquely challenging set of circumstances,” Herlihy said. “It is unusual for us to not be able to gain cooperation with a private entity.”

She noted that before now the agency has had years of collaboration and cooperation with GEO.

“It's not always been a perfect relationship,” she said, adding “but we have collaborated together and we have shared public health goals historically.”

Herlihy’s presence was a symbolic show of support for public health officials in Adams County.

The state and Adams County share public health oversight, under state statutes and regulations, Herlihy said. “When it comes to the public health authority that exists at CDPHE versus at our local public health agencies, it's actually shared authority,” she said. “Our agencies work very closely together, obviously on TB issues, but on all communicable disease issues.”

The event also gave a window into the legal fight.

GEO Group, which runs the facility and others around the country, filed a lawsuit last month against the state to stop enforcement of a new law that requires regular health and safety inspections of immigrant detention facilities.

A federal court judge held a hearing on the case last week in Denver, but has not issued a decision.

Weidenbach said due to the pending litigation it has so far held off suing in order to investigate the TB situation at the detention center in Aurora.

She said if Adams County were to pursue a legal enforcement strategy that would happen in state court. They’ve been told by their legal counsel that the move would likely be met with a stay from a judge while the federal case process plays out.

“There's still a general question that is before the court around public health authority in general,” she said. “So if we were to pursue that right now, that would be paused by the lower court.”

CPR reached out to both GEO and ICE. GEO referred questions to ICE, which has so far not responded to a request for comment.

text:
Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson analyzed Grokipedia’s update records, finding that the site appears to have stopped considering human edits or updating the site since late April. DiResta and Robertson highlighted how Grokipedia’s lack of transparency harms both the site’s reliability and ability to demonstrate the promise of an encyclopedia supported by artificial intelligence (AI).

Kevin Frazier shared a research agenda for understanding the constitutions that govern AI models. Frazier explained that the agenda’s goal is to develop these constitutions in a way that encourages public transparency, oversight, and dialogue that extends beyond the doors of the frontier AI labs.

Nathan Darmon and Tom Reed proposed court-like institutions developed by AI companies to guide frontier models through complex decision-making. Darmon and Reed argued that an evolving set of precedential decisions would be preferable to a static constitutional document because it would create a richer training corpus for models, improve transparency and accountability to the public, and allow for a few careful decisions to guide the models’ actions at scale.

On Scaling Laws, Frazier sat down with Daniel Kokotajlo to discuss Kokotajlo's policy proposal to delay superintelligence, which Kokotajlo thinks is necessary to ensure that the disruptive effects of highly-capable AI systems do not outweigh the benefits. Frazier and Kokotajlo discussed scenario scrutiny, feedback from other AI policy stakeholders, and more.

In the latest edition of the Seriously Risky Business cybersecurity newsletter, Tom Uren discussed North Korea tightening controls on its state-sanctioned hackers, cyberattacks on water facilities in several U.S. states, testing controls on frontier models, and more.

Also on Scaling Laws, DZ Kalman joined Frazier to explore what religious traditions can teach AI governance. They discussed religious responses to AI, Jewish technoculture, kosher supervision as a model for AI certification, the limits of AI use in faith contexts, and how it all connects to debates on alignment, trust, and human dignity.

Camille J. Mackler explained that the executive branch is already using AI for governance in immigration enforcement where legal protections are weak and emphasized that many of the same AI-tools and practices will likely spread beyond immigration, just as post 9/11 surveillance infrastructure did. That trajectory, Mackler argued, makes it urgent to build in transparency and oversight safeguards now, before these systems become further entrenched.

Becca Branum highlighted the underappreciated consequences denying First Amendment protections to AI outputs could have on humans. She explained that existing detection tools can flag AI-like patterns, confirm a file’s history, or verify that a real person exists, but none can establish whether a human is behind a specific piece of text, the factor that determines whether First Amendment protections apply. As a result, Branum argued, platforms and governments are likely to turn to human verification systems which impose additional burdens on users and may compromise privacy.

On Lawfare Daily, Tyler McBrien sat down with Bernice Yeung to discuss Yeung’s recent article about the bumpy history of Big Tech’s relationship with U.S. defense contracting, how Silicon Valley has reshaped the Pentagon, and how, in turn, the Pentagon has reshaped Silicon Valley.

Christy Lopez argued that the Supreme Court’s decision in Chatrie v. United States, holding that the Fourth Amendment applies to geofence searches, is likely to be gradually limited by lower courts, resulting in a more modest win for digital privacy advocates. Instead of relying on courts’ interpretations, Lopez defended the need for legislation at the federal and state level to clarify when and how law enforcement can use their increasing arsenal of digital surveillance tools.

On Lawfare Daily, Kate Klonick spoke with Steve Vladeck about his forthcoming Harvard Law Review Foreword, “The Court Against the Courts,” in which Vladeck argued that the Supreme Court failed to shield district judges from impeachment threats and harassment campaigns and that it bears “significant responsibility” for what’s happened to them.

Peter Beck reported from the first public hearing of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, where Judge Joan Ericksen heard initial statements from the government and respondents about Nazira Haji Zada’s alleged connections to the Islamic State.

On Lawfare Daily, Benjamin Wittes sat down with Peter Harrell, Eric Columbus, Anna Bower, and Roger Parloff to discuss legal challenges to President Trump’s new tariffs, recent motions by James Comey in the ‘86 47 seashell’ prosecution, developments in the Reflecting Pool prosecution, a hearing on Anthropic’s summary judgment motion challenging their supply chain risk designation, and more.

On this week’s Lawfare Live: The Trials of the Trump Administration, Wittes joined Molly Roberts, Columbus, and Parloff to discuss developments in the reflecting pool prosecution, the status of temporary protective status after the Supreme Court’s ruling, litigation over Trump’s executive order on mail-in voting, and more.

Gabor Rona considered the legal implications of events in the U.S. where land in the Israel-occupied West Bank is sold. He argued that promoting such sales constitutes abetting a war crime under international law and that those who participate open themselves up to criminal responsibility under U.S. federal law. Rona also discussed how the sales interact with housing discrimination law and the First Amendment.

Dah-Wei Yih analyzed the constitutional implications of new legislative controls over semiconductor exports proposed by Taiwan’s opposition party. He explained that the proposal would allow lawmakers to review exports themselves, a task traditionally reserved for executive agencies. Yih argued that such a move threatens separation of powers and risks losing expertise in reviews.

On Lawfare Daily, Natalie Orpett spoke with Dara Massicot, Ariane Tabatabai, and Julia Curlee about the short war illusion that is playing out in Ukraine and Iran today and how it could manifest in a future conflict between China and Taiwan.

Peter A. Dutton reviewed Eyck Freymann’s book, “Defending Taiwan: A Strategy to Prevent War With China.” Dutton praised Freymann’s creative approach to deterring China by creating greater political and economic leverage, in addition to traditional military deterrence. He also, however, identified questions Freymann left unanswered, such as whether implementation could happen quickly enough and whether his proposals could accelerate China’s plans for Taiwan.

And on Rational Security, Scott R. Anderson sat down with Curlee, Tabatabai, and Orpett to talk through the week’s big national security news stories, including the most recent updates in the U.S.-Iran war, the confirmation of Jay Clayton as Director of National Security, how the law firm Paul, Weiss has fared since capitulating to Trump, and more.

title: Trump Admin Faces Legal Challenge in Hemispheric Court Over ICE Protest Crackdown
description:
The delegation, represented by Thomas Becker and Nicholas Rodelo, for the University Network for Human Rights, presented evidence of attacks of rights to free assembly and free expression by the Trump administration.
This is the first challenge against the Trump administration on protest crackdowns by an international court, and one of the first legal challenges generally.
“For years, the commission has heard testimony about attacks on protesters carried out by some of the region’s most repressive dictatorships.
We turn to the Inter-American Commission to ask that the commission join us in demanding accountability."
Previously, the IACHR had held proceedings in the context of detainee treatment at Guantánamo Bay, among other cases.
text:
Tuesday, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, or IACHR, at the Organization of American States, a body historically committed to investigating crimes against humanity committed by governments in the Americas, held a hearing in Washington, DC against the Trump administration for its treatment of protests held against Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, crackdowns in the US.

The delegation, represented by Thomas Becker and Nicholas Rodelo, for the University Network for Human Rights, presented evidence of attacks of rights to free assembly and free expression by the Trump administration.

Becker has previously successfully prosecuted a civil lawsuit against former Bolivian President and US ally, Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, over 2003 crackdowns and extrajudicial killings of protesters.

This is the first challenge against the Trump administration on protest crackdowns by an international court, and one of the first legal challenges generally. Speakers included Antonio Romanucci, the attorney representing the family of Renee Good, and former counsel of George Floyd; Reverend David Black, who was struck in the head by federal agents at the Broadview Detention Facility; and Naureen Shah, the director of government affairs at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU).

Speakers and observers at the hearing argued that the commission must be empowered to investigate fully and act decisively, warning that the region is entering a new era of authoritarianism even as many of its democracies remain young and fragile.

During the hearing, video evidence and testimony were presented documenting the alleged abuses, prompting a response from State Department lawyers who argued that the incidents represented isolated cases still under investigation, that the United States has rights the commission should respect, and that the IACHR ought to focus its attention elsewhere in the hemisphere, a suggestion that drew scrutiny given that the US has faced far fewer cases before the commission than many other member states.

State Department representatives further contended that federal agents operating under significant stress could not be expected to act "perfectly," and maintained that any agents found to have violated standards would face penalties, though they were unable to answer specific questions from commissioners about ongoing cases or offer evidence of any such penalties actually being imposed, saying only that they would "write down" the questions and respond later.

The commission and the civil society delegation renewed a request—thus far denied by Washington—for an IACHR delegation to visit the United States, likely Chicago, to assess conditions on the ground.

Petitioners also singled out National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 (NSPM-7) as a central mechanism of the crackdown, arguing it chills freedom of expression by recasting protesters and dissidents, including anti-capitalist, "anti-Christian," and anti-fascist activists, as "terrorists." Blacklists of prominent leftist actors have also been compiled, with state resources used to prosecute them. "This is the new McCarthyism," the delegation added.

They pointed out that resources once dedicated to investigating internal abuse by immigration enforcement agents have instead been slashed, citing an internal FBI memo halting investigations into Department of Homeland Security officers, and that officials tasked with oversight are now regarded within the agencies as "internal adversaries" rather than watchdogs.

"These are the exact same tactics used by Latin American dictatorships from the 1970s," said Becker. "These tactics have been propped up by the US for decades, and are now coming back here, to be used against Americans," he added. The commission was created in the wake of the rise of military dictatorships in Latin America, backed by the US during the Cold War, including Augusto Pinochet in Chile, Rafael Videla in Argentina, and Hugo Banzer in Bolivia.

Becker also argued, "This is not the first time that agents backed by the US government target priests," alluding to the past abuses and killings of religious opposition leaders in Central America.

Speaking to Drop Site News, Dr. James Cavallaro, former president of IACHR and law faculty at Columbia, Stanford, and Harvard, added that "there is a conviction from those in power that they can suppress dissent" and rule through power and violence to "impose their ideology," where "opposition must be crushed."

This is the first time the commission has held any hearing of this type concerning domestic repression against the US government, which was the main force behind the founding and funding of the IACHR and the Organization of American States (OAS). “For years, the commission has heard testimony about attacks on protesters carried out by some of the region’s most repressive dictatorships. Now, it is the United States that will be called to answer for these abuses,” said Cavallaro.

The US government, including figures in the current administration like Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has historically been supportive of the IACHR and the OAS, but may see the IACHR as a new target, as it continues its campaign against international legal organizations including the International Criminal Court.

Locke Bowman, attorney for Reverend David Black, shared, "What happened to Rev. Black was emblematic of the physical abuse that ICE and CBP [Customs and Border Patrol] officers directed at conscientious folks in Chicago, Minneapolis, Portland, and elsewhere around the country who bore witness to the Trump administration's cruel immigration policies with their voices, their prayers, and their cellphone cameras."

He added: "There has been no accountability whatsoever for the officers responsible for the pervasive violations of free speech and human dignity. We turn to the Inter-American Commission to ask that the commission join us in demanding accountability."

At the hearing, the University Network for Human Rights also published a detailed report, submitted as part of its formal petition to the commission, laying out documented instances of excessive force, free expression violations, and lack of accountability tied to the crackdown on ICE protests.

The commission is now expected to weigh whether the evidence and testimony presented warrant further inquiry, including a possible on-the-ground visit to the United States, before issuing findings or referring the matter further within the inter-American human rights system.

The last hearing against the US government, sponsored by the ACLU, was held in the context of dozens of extrajudicial killings by US forces in the Caribbean and Pacific, against "drug boats," which experts say violate US and international law, violate local sovereignty, and kill civilians without due process, all without helping to solve the drug crisis. Previously, the IACHR had held proceedings in the context of detainee treatment at Guantánamo Bay, among other cases.

Speakers and observers at the hearing argued that the commission must be empowered to investigate fully and act decisively, warning that the region is entering a new era of authoritarianism even as many of its democracies remain young and fragile. Crime and migration are increasingly being used as pretexts to suspend democratic norms, enabling interference in elections; extrajudicial killings; bans on opposition parties; declared states of exception; suspended protest rights; the jailing of dissidents; militarized policing; and the dismantling of checks on military, intelligence, and presidential power.

text:
By Steve Gorman

Aug 7 (Reuters) - New Jersey civil rights officials have opened an investigation into the treatment of detainees at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in ‌Newark run by the private prison company GEO Group, the state attorney general said ‌on Friday.

A statement announcing delivery of investigative subpoenas in the civil rights probe of Delaney Hall came after a man ​from El Salvador, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, died in custody on Saturday after suffering what ICE called a medical emergency.

Delaney Hall earlier this year was the scene of protests that led to clashes between demonstrators and law enforcement personnel.

The man's family on Tuesday accused facility operators of failing to provide vital medical attention to ‌Lopez-Cornejo, who they said suffered ⁠from health issues such as high blood pressure, diabetes and epilepsy, and relied on several medications to keep those conditions under control.

His mother, Maria Cornejo, said ⁠her son had called the day before his death and told her he lost feeling in half his face and arm. Relatives demanded an independent investigation of his death.

ICE said Lopez-Cornejo received proper medical care ​and was ​seen by health professionals.

The newly launched state investigation "will focus ​on whether any action or inaction ‌by GEO Group employees violated the civil rights of people detained at the facility," Attorney General Jennifer Davenport's office said in the statement.

There was no immediate reply from ICE, the Department of Homeland Security or GEO Group to requests by Reuters for comment.

Delaney Hall, a 1,000-bed facility, has been a flashpoint for protests over complaints of spoiled food, squalid, unsanitary bathroom conditions, faulty ventilation and inadequate ‌medical care. Two local Democratic politicians helping to spearhead ​the demonstrations, U.S. Representative LaMonica McIver and Mayor Ras Baraka, ​were arrested outside the facility in May ​in what they said were politically motivated acts of intimidation.

Democratic New Jersey Governor ‌Mikie Sherrill later ordered state police to assume ​control of the area ​around Delaney after increasingly tense face-offs between protesters and federal officers at the jail.

Complaints have been lodged against other migrant detention centers, with more than 50 people dying in ICE ​custody nationwide since President Donald Trump ‌returned to office in January of last year and launched a sweeping deportation campaign.

(Reporting ​and writing by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Additional reporting by Kanishka Singh in ​Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Chris Reese)
