text:
With this series of updates, WOLA seeks to cover the most important developments at the U.S.-Mexico border. See past updates here.

Your donation to WOLA is crucial to keeping these paywall-free and ad-free Updates going. Please contribute now and support our work.

THIS WEEK IN BRIEF:

Border wall updates: Construction equipment has appeared in Big Bend National Park as businesses and members of Congress demand more information. Drought-hit New Mexico ranchers stopped wall-builders from pumping water, while protesters in Arizona are trying to save a 200-year-old cottonwood tree.

Administration revokes legal aid contracts for unaccompanied children: A contract to provide non-profit legal representation to unaccompanied children expired on July 31; the new, smaller legal service provider is a Trump administration-connected Texas law firm. Many children, of all ages, will now have to face immigration judges alone to defend their asylum claims and avoid deportation.

More deaths in ICE custody as “mass deportation” ratchets up: The 23rd person to die in ICE custody perished on August 1. Other deaths are not being reported, as ICE is releasing them while they are in medical distress. Some detained people are being force-fed when they go on hunger strikes to protest conditions. ICE has detained over 600,000 people since the Trump administration began, and arrested at least 46,000 in July, a monthly record. CBP is hiring contractors to chase down deported migrants in their home countries, in an attempt to collect fines from them.

Impacts around the Americas: Temporary Protected Status for about 350,000 Haitian citizens is now terminated, following a June Supreme Court ruling. The first deportation plane since devastating June earthquakes—which included freshly deported people among the victims—landed in Venezuela. Reports inform about how “safe third country” agreements are being used to end asylum cases; deportation flights; and impacts of U.S. migration policies in Guatemala, Brazil, Uruguay, Mexico, Belize, and Nicaragua.

THE FULL UPDATE:

Border wall updates

Construction equipment arrives in Big Bend National Park

Video recorded on August 6 showed bulldozers clearing native vegetation in Big Bend National Park, a jewel of the U.S. National Park system along the Rio Grande in remote west Texas. Contractors are apparently clearing an access road as part of a border barrier-building project in the park, enabled by the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) waivers of environmental laws. Southwest Valley Constructors, a subsidiary of the Kiewit Corporation, appears to have moved from planning to construction under a $1.7 billion contract to build access roads, 17 miles of vehicle barriers (not tall bollard border walls), lighting, and other infrastructure in the park.

Sam Karas, “More Questions Than Answers as Contractors Descend Upon Big Bend National Park” (Big Bend Sentinel, August 4, 2026).

Over the past few weeks, observers on the ground have spotted survey crews on roads along the river and staging areas popping up north of the park — but officials still don’t have straight answers for many of the questions anxious locals have

Travis Bubenik, Zoe Kurland, “Border Project Contractors Arrive in Big Bend National Park as Texas Lawmakers Call for a Pause” (Marfa Public Radio, August 4, 2026).

On Tuesday, Marfa Public Radio witnessed a bulldozer and multiple trucks bearing the contractor’s name – Southwest Valley Constructors – stationed inside the park near the entrance to Cottonwood Campground, which is situated right next to the U.S.-Mexico border.

A coalition of more than 140 tourism outfitters and other businesses active in and near the park sent a letter to Texas’s Republican governor and two senators urging them to block physical barriers in favor of technology-only solutions. “Big Bend has been called ‘Texas’ Gift to the Nation’ and generations of Texans have built their lives on this river,” they wrote. “We are asking you, our elected representatives, to protect our livelihoods, our river, and one of our state’s most treasured landscapes from needless and permanent destruction.”

The letter offers a new data point about how rare border crossings are in this region. Border Patrol’s migrant apprehensions inside the park’s 118 miles (about 6 percent of the entire U.S.-Mexico border) made up just 0.045 percent of border-wide apprehensions in fiscal 2025: 200 people out of a total of 443,671.

The ability to waive environmental, public health, and historic preservation laws to build border walls, granted by a provision in the REAL ID Act of 2005, specifies that the waivers are for “areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” WOLA’s Adam Isacson submitted an “Expert Report,” documenting the very low and infrequent nature of illegal entries in the Big Bend Sector, to the court considering a local challenge to the Big Bend construction project.

Dan Gooding, “Texas Businesses Issue Warning to Republicans About Trump’s Border Barriers” (Newsweek, August 4, 2026).

The business leaders are warning that much of Big Bend’s tourism could be lost if access to the Rio Grande is cut off

Twelve House Democrats, most from Texas, wrote to senior Trump administration officials requesting detailed plans about the project in the national park. The letter raises concerns about potential damage from building a road on Mariscal Mountain, where the river makes its “big bend.” Not among the signers was Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), who represents a border district and is the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Homeland Security Subcommittee.

Rep. Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), “Texas Democratic Congressional Delegation & Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Urge Answers Before Action Jeopardizing Big Bend” (U.S. House of Representatives, July 31, 2026).

Delay work on a proposed road across and over Big Bend National Park’s Mariscal Mountain until specific details of the project are made fully available and questions answered about the potentially irreparable destruction the project poses

A development board in the nearby border town of Presidio had gone to federal court to block construction there, contending that border wall building would harm the municipal levee system in an area where floods are common. Citing the federal government’s authority to waive other laws to build walls, Washington, DC District Court Judge Reggie Walton declined, on August 2, to block construction while deliberations proceed.

DHS attorneys argued that the border wall will increase security in Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, and that the Department’s goal is zero illegal border crossings. Walton replied, “You’re never going to get that.”

Rebecca Santana, “A Federal Judge Lets DHS Proceed With a Border Wall Through a Small Texas Town’s Levee System” (Associated Press, Associated Press, August 3, 2026).

A federal judge has ruled that the Department of Homeland Security can proceed with building a border wall through a levee system in a small Texas town

Mary Cantrell, “Judge Declines to Block Big Bend Area Border Wall” (Marfa Public Radio, August 2, 2026).

A federal judge on Sunday rejected a Presidio, Texas entity’s request to block construction over claims that the Trump administration violated the Rivers and Harbors Act in pursuing the border wall build near the city’s levee system

On July 31, the Texas state government’s General Land Office (GLO) formally reprimanded Montana-based Barnard Construction for illegally clearing more than a mile of state land in Presidio County without authorization. GLO Commissioner Dawn Buckingham ordered both Barnard and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to halt work and restore the land, a rare rebuke of the Trump administration on a border issue from Texas’s deeply pro-Trump state government.

Sam Karas, “Border Wall Contractors Ordered to Stop Unauthorized Work on State Land” (Big Bend Sentinel, July 31, 2026).

Montana-based firm Barnard Construction was formally reprimanded by the Texas General Land Office (GLO) on Friday morning after the company illegally cleared more than a mile-long swath of land for border wall construction. The agency’s cease-and-desist marks the first time a State of Texas entity has made any statement on the border

More waivers

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin signed a waiver, which took effect on July 27, suspending dozens of laws in Border Patrol’s Big Bend and Del Rio sectors, stretching several hundred miles from the Big Bend region to Lake Amistad east of Laredo.

“DHS Waives Environmental Laws for Border Barriers and Roads From Big Bend to Lake Amistad” (Houston Public Media, July 29, 2026).

The waiver clears the way for barriers, roads and surveillance infrastructure, though federal officials have not specified what will be built throughout the project area

Flood risks

On the other side of Texas, in Starr County, residents of the border town of San Ygnacio say that plans to build border wall and border buoys could increase hazards in a historic floodplain that experienced destructively high waters in mid-July. That flooding damaged a pump that supplies San Ygnacio’s drinking water.

Sandra Sanchez, “Border Residents Say the Wall Is Being Built on Long-Established Flood Plains” (Border Report, August 3, 2026).

Sandra Sanchez, “Texas Floodwaters Inundate Areas Cleared for Border Wall Construction” (Border Report, July 23, 2026).

Mt. Cristo Rey

Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas), who represents El Paso, introduced legislation that would prohibit construction on Mt. Cristo Rey, the mountain (technically in New Mexico) that straddles the border and dominates views on El Paso’s western edge. Escobar’s bill, which is unlikely to move in a Republican-majority House of Representatives, prohibits the federal government from using eminent domain to seize land on the mountain, much of which is owned by the Catholic Diocese of Las Cruces, New Mexico.

Camillo Barone, “Texas Lawmaker Introduces Bill to Protect Mount Cristo Rey From Border Wall Construction” (National Catholic Reporter, July 29, 2026).

Religious men and women in the borderland region accompany migrants on a daily basis in the federal courthouses and in immigration detention centers, seeking to provide solace, comfort and support

New Mexico well-drilling stopped

In drought-stricken southern New Mexico, CBP ordered border wall construction crews to stop drilling unpermitted wells, used primarily to mix cement and tamp down dust, after ranchers protested that the pumping—up to 300 gallons per minute—was threatening livestock water supplies.

Mikella Schuettler, “Contractors Building Border Wall Ordered to Stop Drilling Wells in Drought-Stricken New Mexico” (Associated Press, Associated Press, August 5, 2026).

Customs and Border Protection has ordered construction crews building Trump’s second border wall to stop drilling wells in drought-stricken New Mexico after ranchers said pumping the groundwater needed to mix cement could threaten their livestock

Peter O’dowd, “As Anger Mounts, Feds Tell Border Wall Contractors to Stop Drilling for Water in New Mexico” (WBUR (NPR Boston), August 5, 2026).

Ranchers along the U.S.-Mexico border are outraged that the federal government is drilling unpermitted wells to pump water from the region’s drought-stricken aquifers

Mikella Schuettler, “Ranchers Win Fight as Trump Halts Border Wall Water Drilling in Drought-Hit New Mexico” (The Independent (UK), Yahoo!, August 4, 2026).

Customs and Border Protection has ordered construction crews building Trump’s second border wall to stop drilling wells in drought-stricken New Mexico

Coral Murphy Marcos, “Crews Building Trump Border Wall in Drought-Hit New Mexico Ordered to Stop Drilling Wells” (The Guardian (Uk), August 3, 2026).

Residents and farmers say contractors have tapped border aquifers that threaten water supply for those nearby

Cottonwood trees in Arizona

In Lochiel, in southeastern Arizona’s remote San Rafael Valley, protesters are staging a sustained “tree sit” in the path of a planned secondary wall being built by contractor Fisher Sand and Gravel. On July 27, contractors crushed three ancient cottonwood trees—some locals call them “grandmothers”—with excavators. Protesters are now defending a single 200-year-old cottonwood estimated to be the last of its kind on the border.

Douglas Main, “Protesters Occupy 200-Year-Old Tree at US-Mexico Border to Stop Its Destruction: ‘She’s Our Statue of Liberty’” (The Guardian (Uk), August 4, 2026).

Demonstrators stage ‘tree sit’ in Arizona town to stop felling of ancient cottonwood grove to make way for border wall

Michael Loria, “Activists Defend Century-Old Tree Standing in Way of Trump’s Border Wall” (USA Today, July 28, 2026).

The tree is the last remaining of four cottonwoods that have stood along the U.S.-Mexico border in Lochiel, Arizona, for between an estimated 100 to 200 years. Border Patrol says the trees must be removed for the wall

Michael Loria, “Sierra Club Says Century-Old Trees Felled to Make Way for Border Wall” (USA Today, July 27, 2026).

Locals say the trees have served as a community gathering place for generations and are ecologically rare

Tohono O’Odham nation faces wall-building it has long opposed

CBP began planning construction on 62 miles of Tohono O’odham reservation land, which straddles south-central Arizona and Mexico’s state of Sonora, without seeking the Nation’s authorization. Nation attorneys argued at a July 22 hearing in Washington that DHS lacks authority to unilaterally diminish reservation boundaries, a power that belongs to Congress. DHS is citing its REAL ID Act waiver authority.

Cheyenne Mcneill, “DHS Wants to Build a Border Wall Through Tohono O’odham Land. It’s Another Instance of the US Undermining Tribal Sovereignty.” (Mother Jones, August 3, 2026).

The nation says the wall would be “devastating” to its lands and people

Arlyssa D. Becenti, “Trump Border Wall Would Illegally Reduce Tribal Lands, Leaders Argue” (Arizona Republic, The Arizona Daily Star, July 26, 2026).

The Tohono O’odham Nation asks a federal court to halt border wall construction across tribal lands, citing sovereignty, sacred sites and environmental harm

Administration revokes legal aid contracts for unaccompanied children

On July 31, the Trump administration allowed the Acacia Center for Justice’s federal contract to provide legal representation to migrant children who arrived unaccompanied—covering nearly 100 legal providers representing approximately 20,000 children—to expire, while owing providers more than $65 million in unpaid invoices dating to November 2025. Acacia declined a bridge contract that would have required providers to turn over confidential client information, calling it an ethics violation that could have enabled deportations.

In El Paso, Estrella del Paso shut down its Unaccompanied Children’s Program on July 31, laying off 13 employees and leaving 243 children without representation in far west Texas and New Mexico. Estrella is owed nearly $1 million for services already rendered. ProBar in south Texas laid off 20 percent of its staff. At least 40 law firms and service providers have been forced to lay off staff or suspend services across the network.

The administration’s replacement, announced August 4, is a $150 million contract awarded to Burke Law Group—a 26-employee Houston boutique firm that bills itself as specializing in “high-stakes litigation, environmental, regulatory, and corporate matters.” Only two of its lawyers list any immigration law experience in their backgrounds. The firm’s founder served in the first Trump administration.

“We know what happens to children that go to court without an attorney. In one word, it is deportation,” said Estrella del Paso’s executive director, Melissa Lopez. Research confirms that without legal representation, children brought before judges—often too young to understand the proceedings—win immigration relief less than 1 percent of the time. Immigration judges removing unaccompanied minors issued over 18,000 removal orders in June alone, a 73 percent increase from January.

“We’re going to see a lot of kids railroaded into taking voluntary departure, aka self-deport, even where their protection needs are acute and where they would be facing real danger to their lives in their countries of origin,” said Acacia Center Executive Director Shaina Aber.

The Acacia Center’s public statement documented the human costs through anonymized case profiles: a deaf, non-verbal, autistic child kidnapped during his journey; trafficking survivors; a 2-year-old whose attorney has continued representing her despite receiving no government funding because it would be “unconscionable for a 2-year-old to be alone in court.” The International Rescue Committee announced it would continue representing unaccompanied children despite the loss of funding.

Cybele Mayes-Osterman, Rebecca Santana, Ryan J. Foley, Valerie Gonzalez, “A $150m Contract for Migrant Kids’ Lawyers Goes to a Trump-Linked Texas Firm, Raising Concerns” (Associated Press, Associated Press, August 5, 2026).

Legal aid groups are raising concerns after the Trump administration awarded a $150 million contract to a small Texas law firm with limited experience in immigration law

Gina Christian, “Diocese of El Paso Ends Unaccompanied Child Ministry as Trump Admin Withholds Almost $1m Owed” (National Catholic Reporter, August 4, 2026).

Eric Bazail-Eimil, “26-Employee Texas Law Firm Gets $150m to Represent 24,000 Children in Immigration Court” (Politico, August 4, 2026).

None of the Burke Law Group’s lawyers list immigration law as an area of expertise, per the firm’s website

Mary Ellen Klas, “Immigrant Kids Deserve to Keep Their Lawyers” (Bloomberg, August 4, 2026).

The Department of Health and Human Services ended the contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, leaving more than 20,000 unaccompanied kids in legal limbo

“Statement From Acacia Center for Justice in Response to Trump Administration’s False Claims” (Acacia Center for Justice, August 4, 2026).

The administration doesn’t get to manufacture a crisis, offer an unacceptable “fix”, and then claim it’s solved. More than 20,000 unaccompanied children are waiting for a real solution

Cindy Ramirez, “Estrella del Paso Shuts Down Unaccompanied Children’s Program as Trump Ends Funding” (El Paso Matters, July 31, 2026).

The nonprofit, a ministry of the Catholic Diocese of El Paso, provided free and reduced legal services to unaccompanied migrant children. Without federal funding, the organization shut down its children’s program and laid off 13 employees Friday

Rebecca Santana, Valerie Gonzalez, “Thousands of Migrant Children in the US Could Face New Deportation Risks as Legal Aid Deal Expires” (Associated Press, Associated Press, July 31, 2026).

Migrant children who came to the U.S. alone could soon face immigration court without legal representation

Gwynne Hogan, “Inside the NYC Courtroom Where Detained Children Face Deportation Without Attorneys” (The City Reporter, July 31, 2026).

Around 20,000 unaccompanied minors nationwide are set to lose legal services when the federal government ends a contract Friday. One NYC immigration court shows us what that will look like

Arelis R. Hernandez, “Thousands of Immigrant Children May Soon Face a Judge Alone” (The Washington Post, July 30, 2026).

A federal contract that provides attorneys for vulnerable undocumented minors is set to expire Friday. Advocates fear children will be left to defend themselves in court alone

Jackie Llanos, “More Migrant Kids Are Getting Removal Orders. Some Could Lose Their Attorneys Too.” (NOTUS, July 29, 2026).

A contract for nonprofits representing thousands of children is set to expire Friday

More deaths in ICE custody as “mass deportation” ratchets up

23rd death this year

At least 53 people have died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) system of mostly contractor-run detention centers since the Trump administration began. The 23rd in-custody death of the 2026 calendar year happened on August 1: Edwin Jeovanny Lopez Cornejo, a 39-year-old citizen of El Salvador, died at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall Detention Facility in Newark. Delaney Hall, run by the private contractor GEO Group, has been the site of frequent protests as detainees have recounted inhumane conditions and medical neglect. Lopez Cornejo, a landscaper and father of a 12-year-old U.S. citizen daughter, was detained on June 18 after 20 years in the United States and filed a habeas petition on July 24 challenging his detention on medical grounds.

ICE did not publicly report another recent Delaney Hall death, Rep. Robert Menendez (D-New Jersey) revealed, because the agency had technically “released” the deceased person while in the middle of a medical emergency. Under a June ICE change to a 2021 policy, it is no longer reporting to Congress the deaths of people within 30 days of their release, as it was compelled to do before.

29-year-old Mexican citizen Priciliano Trejo died in a Georgia hospital on July 24 after being released from ICE’s Stewart Detention Center. He suffered from leukemia, and advocates allege that he was denied necessary medical care while in custody. His death was not reported as occurring “in custody” because ICE released him to the hospital while he was still alive. The agency’s policy change will complicate efforts to keep an accurate count of in-custody deaths.

Matt Shuham, “Congressman Makes Stunning Allegation After Visiting ICE’s Delaney Hall” (The Huffington Post, August 4, 2026).

Rep. Rob Menendez made a stunning allegation while addressing the recent death of another man who had been detained at Delaney Hall

Gwynne Hogan, “Salvadoran Man Held at Delaney Hall Dies in ICE Custody” (The City Reporter, August 3, 2026).

The detainee had an extensive medical history, including epilepsy, according to a lawsuit. He had complained about his face and hand going numb just before his death, his mother said

Ana Ley, Mark Bonamo, Tracey Tully, “Immigrant Held at Delaney Detention Center Has Died, Officials Say” (The New York Times, August 3, 2026).

The mayor of Newark identified the dead man as Edwin Lopez-Cornejo. The New Jersey center has been the focus of intense scrutiny for its treatment of detainees

Top DHS statistician departs

The outgoing executive director of the Office of Homeland Security Statistics is one of very few federal officials to speak out against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown

Checkpoint operations that used to be “very limited” have resumed with higher staffing, and one local checkpoint could soon get an infusion of money

ICE vehicle pursuits in Rio Grande Valley

Immigration agents sped after a vehicle through a residential neighborhood on the same day of the agency’s traffic stop pause, reportedly endangering a mother and son—before pulling a gun on and briefly handcuffing a U.S. citizen

New asylum rule enables quick case dismissals

A rule introduced July 28, effective immediately with the comment period still pending, transfers 444,724 pending USCIS asylum cases directly to immigration courts for removal proceedings, skipping the asylum officer review stage. Maria Sacchetti, “Asylum Seekers Could Be Sent Directly to Deportation Court Under New Rule” (The Washington Post, July 28, 2026).

The Trump administration rule, which took effect immediately, could transfer nearly 450,000 cases to immigration judges, who could dismiss the asylum petitions

A new rule for asylum applications adds to the bevy of changes under the Trump administration to the core program for those fleeing persecution in their home countries

Expanding family separation

A Migration Policy Institute analysis documented the second Trump administration’s ongoing wave of family separations, which is larger but far less visible than the 2018 “zero-tolerance” crisis. Approximately 205,000 children, 71 percent of them U.S. citizens, had a parent detained by immigration officials as of May 2026, per Brookings Institution estimates. Of 320,000 fiscal year 2026 ICE book-ins, nearly 17,900 (6%) involved people who self-reported as parents of U.S.-citizen children. That is almost twice fiscal 2024 levels, and likely a significant undercount.

ICE has reportedly used the threat of separation as leverage to induce voluntary departure, MPI reported, offering parents the choice to leave with their children or contest removal and see their children transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) as unaccompanied minors.

Because they are happening in a more decentralized, opaque, and often indirect way, “the public response has been more muted” as family separations continue to mount.

Greg Garcia, Muzaffar Chishti, “In Its Second Term, Trump Administration Quietly Expands Family Separation” (Migration Policy Institute, July 30, 2026).

Immigration enforcement during the second Trump term is driving a quieter, more diffuse wave of family separations inside the United States, often through detention, deportation, and pressures to depart the country voluntarily

Another Migration Policy Institute analysis estimated the U.S. unauthorized immigrant population, finding that it reached 15.8 million as of mid-2024, a historic peak after holding stable near 11 million throughout the 2010s. (The U.S. population was estimated at 342 million a year ago.)

Mexico’s share has fallen from 62% in 2010 to 35% in 2024, while Central American (up 2.3 million) and South American (up 1.3 million, led by Venezuela and Colombia) populations rose sharply.

MPI noted that up to 40% of the 2024 unauthorized population—approximately 6.3 million people—held some form of “twilight” legal status (TPS, DACA, humanitarian parole, pending asylum). Officials at Ft. Bliss, Texas, opened two of 10 new barracks created with 3D-printers ahead of the 101st Airborne deployment

At the New York Review of Books, journalist Julia Preston reviewed Jazmine Ulloa’s book El Paso: Five Families and One Hundred Years of Blood, Migration, Race, and Memory, which tells the story of El Paso, Texas, and its complex history of migration, violence, and “how resilient immigrants and Mexican Americans have contributed to the economic progress of the borderlands and their continuously evolving multiethnic mix, despite the United States’ efforts, generation after generation, to build walls and jails to thwart the flow of people.”

Five construction workers were detained by members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement during a traffic stop on Friday in Londonderry, according to officials from Migrant Justice. Community members say it happened along Route 11.

Members of the Londonderry community say they were caught by surprise Friday morning, when advocates reported immigration enforcement, in their town.

"This was very open on the state highway and right in the middle of town, so this is kind of shock," said Thom Simmons, the executive director of Neighborhood Connections, a local social service organization in Londonderry.

Multiple people in town told NBC5 that they have heard of ICE agents in surrounding communities, including Manchester. But they haven't seen any federal agents in Londonderry until Friday.

"This is definitely a first. I have heard of them being in Manchester and further north, but not here," said South Londonderry resident Mimi Wright.

Until Friday morning, when federal agents detained five construction workers during a traffic stop. A video obtained from advocate group Migrant Justice shows unmarked vehicles pulled over in Londonderry and several federal agents standing on the roadway.

Simmons said their organization received multiple calls from upset community members throughout the morning, alerting them about the incident.

"Everyone I have mentioned this to has had an immediate reaction of anger and shock that this is going on here in our community. It gets people very unsettled, very upset. You know, clenched fist type reactions. As to why- why is this still happening," he said.

Neighborhood Connections will hold a public meeting on Saturday to discuss the incident as a community. It was organized by a Southern Vermont resident and State Representative Chris Morrow.

"It's really for the purpose of one disseminating accurate information. What actually happened and what is rumor mill? And then to allow the community just to express themselves as to how they feel," Simmons said.

Saturday's public meeting is scheduled for 10am at the Neighborhood Connections building in the Mountain Marketplace plaza.

NBC5 also reached out to ICE for comment but has not heard back.

text:
WILMINGTON, N.C.—On Thursday, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina denied qualified immunity for officers who raided an innocent family’s Pender County home in April 2024. The lawsuit brought against the officers and their government employers by Avery Marshall, Alisa Carr and their attorneys from the Institute for Justice (IJ) can now move forward.

“This decision is a massive first step toward getting justice for Avery and Alisa after they were subjected to a terrifying raid that never should have happened,” said IJ Attorney Marie Miller. “When officers overlook obvious evidence they’re raiding the wrong house, they must be held accountable. And when law-enforcement officers destroy innocent people’s property trying to catch a criminal, the public as a whole must foot the bill—not the unlucky innocent homeowners.”

In April 2024, officers from the Lee and Pender County Sheriff’s Departments were looking for a suspect accused of stealing from parked cars in various counties. They believed the suspect’s phone pinged off a cell tower near Avery and Alisa’s home in the small hamlet of Willard. But many homes and other properties were within the radius of where the ping occurred, and police decided to raid Avery and Alisa’s home simply because there was a Nissan parked out front, and they believed the suspect had been driving a Nissan. But the Nissan the officers believed the suspect had been riding in was a different model than Alisa’s, was ten years newer, had a different VIN number and license plate number, and was registered to the suspect or a relative, not Alisa.

Instead of verifying any of those facts, the officers conducted a heavily-armed midnight raid, terrorizing a sleeping family, smashing windows and doors, throwing a flashbang grenade into the home, reinjuring Avery’s recently operated on back, causing Alisa heart palpitations, and holding the couple’s 9-and-16-year-old children at gun point. After searching every nook and cranny of the home, officers left it in shambles. The suspect was apprehended the next day in a different county.

“That night caused our family so much trauma and pain, so we’re very happy that our lawsuit against those responsible for it can move forward,” said Avery. “What happened to our family should never happen to anyone.”

In Thursday’s decision, the court held that the officer who applied for a warrant to search Alisa and Avery’s home was not entitled to qualified immunity for falsely swearing to a judge that officers had observed the suspect’s vehicle at Alisa and Avery’s home. The court also denied qualified immunity to the individual officers who conducted the raid, for two reasons: First, the officers violated the knock-and-announce rule—by intruding into the home less than a minute after arriving in the middle of the night, without adequately announcing their presence and reasonably allowing the occupants to open the door. Second, the officers kept searching the home after explicitly observing “that ain’t the car” the suspect had been associated with. As the court explained, the officers, “should have discontinued the search after realizing errors in the warrant.” The court also allowed the federal and state constitutional takings claims to proceed against the sheriff’s offices for the damage they caused to the home.

The court gave the defendants 14 days from the order’s date to answer Alisa and Avery’s complaint.

text:
After more than an hour of pointed criticism lobbed at the Gunnison County Sheriff's Office earlier this week, a policy change was made.

“We're done dealing with ICE. You guys talk me into it. I'm done dealing with them,” Gunnison County Sheriff Adam Murdie said at a County Commissioners meeting.

Murdie bore the brunt of intense criticism from Gunnison County residents who took to the regularly scheduled meeting to voice displeasure with immigration enforcement in the county. They accused the sheriff's office of alerting ICE when undocumented residents were at the Gunnison County Jail, leading to their detainment upon release from local custody.

Residents who addressed the commission estimated that around 60 people have been picked up by ICE from Gunnison County, an area with a total population of just more than 17,000. Murdie, who was elected to sheriff as an unaffiliated candidate, said he did not come to the decision lightly.

“It's a position that I've been put in that I struggle with between my humanity, my job, and trying to do the best thing I can do for the community of Gunnison, Colorado,” Muride said.

The sheriff also alluded to concerns that not cooperating with federal immigration agents could lead to worse outcomes for the community.

“I am so afraid of what's going to happen when they find out that we're not allowing them to come do their job. They're going to come into this community and just run rampant like they do everywhere else,” Murdie told the room.

The jurisdictional challenge is the latest in a growing trend of local law enforcement seeking to find ways to do their jobs amid the increased focus on immigration enforcement. President Donald Trump campaigned on tougher immigration policies and mass deportations. In Colorado, some district attorneys have complained those deportations have undermined the local justice system. In places like Durango, law enforcement have had to monitor protests against federal immigration agents and in Mesa County, the sheriff’s office had to investigate a deputy for communicating with federal agents in a way that violated state law.

Local officials see limited options

All three of the Gunnison County Commissioners voiced frustration about the position the county was in. Gunnison County Commissioner Laura Puckett Daniels told the crowd, Tuesday, that the last 18 months “have been a time of incredible uncertainty and turmoil.”

“My first two years as county commissioner were not under the Trump administration, and I took for granted what it was like to have a working federal government and a working federal partner,” Puckett Daniels said.

Puckett Dainels added that she recognized the difficult position the sheriff was in, given the ICE enforcement operations in places like Minnesota where two Americans were shot by ICE officers.

“Many of you have probably heard me say I grew up in St. Paul, Minnesota. I had friends on the front lines of the ICE invasion of the Twin Cities. It feels very, very personal, even if we haven't had an ICE invasion of Gunnison County,” Puckett Daniels said.

Commissioner Jonathan Houck said some of the Gunnison residents removed by ICE in recent months were people he knew.

“I do a lot of head scratching about wondering what and why the removal for our community was facilitated and how legal or how just or, even at the most basic human level, how moral that is,” Houck said.

The interplay between local and federal law enforcement on immigration has received significant scrutiny in recent months. The state of Colorado passed laws limiting what information local law enforcement can share with federal immigration authorities. Those laws led to one deputy in Mesa County resigning after he was sued by the state for alerting ICE agents about an undocumented college student driving on Interstate 70.

County jails do sometimes notify immigration agents that an inmate they’ve inquired about is set to be released. Gunnison County Undersheriff Josh Ashe said the office’s previous policies were in line with state law.

“We had not done anything that was not legally within our bounds to do. Yes, I understand everybody was upset that we had made the notifications with ICE that were legally acceptable to do. But the way we saw it as being law enforcement is community safety,” Ashe said.

The commissioners commended the sheriff’s office for being responsive to the public. Houck said this period of increased federal action made for a uniquely challenging time in local government, noting that actions at the federal level were rarely felt as acutely in Gunnison County as the recent immigration push has been.

“We've been lucky to live in a bubble for a long time,” he said. “And our bubble's been getting a little burst these days.”

text:
TRENTON – Attorney General Jennifer Davenport today announced the issuance of investigative subpoenas by the New Jersey Division on Civil Rights (DCR) regarding Delaney Hall in Newark, a private immigration detention facility owned and operated by The GEO Group, Inc. The Office’s investigation will focus on whether any action or inaction by GEO Group employees violated the civil rights of people detained at the facility, in the wake of reports of alarming conditions and recent deaths. Individuals with information relevant to this civil rights investigation can contact DCR’s Affirmative Enforcement Unit at AffirmativeEnforcement@njcivilrights.gov.

“New Jersey has a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people in our State,” said Attorney General Davenport. “For detained individuals, including those held by a private corporation like GEO Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care. We will take every action available under law to safeguard these core legal principles. We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected.”

“Ensuring that civil rights are upheld in all environments — particularly in settings where individuals may be vulnerable — is a fundamental responsibility,” said Yolanda N. Melville, Director of the Division on Civil Rights. “Our investigation will be thorough, impartial, and guided by the requirements and protections established by New Jersey law.”

If violations are found, as with any civil rights investigation, the Office will initiate appropriate civil enforcement action as provided for under the New Jersey Civil Rights Act (NJCRA) and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD).

Today’s announcement comes as litigation continues between the New Jersey Department of Health (DOH) and GEO Group. The Attorney General filed that lawsuit on behalf of DOH this past June, seeking a court order requiring GEO Group to grant the agency access to Delaney Hall to conduct health inspections.

***

The New Jersey Division on Civil Rights is responsible for preventing and eliminating discrimination and bias-based harassment in employment, housing, and places of public accommodation. DCR enforces the LAD, the New Jersey Family Leave Act, the Fair Chance in Housing Act, the John Lewis Voter Empowerment Act, and the NJCRA.

The NJCRA protects individuals against the deprivation of rights. The law authorizes the Attorney General and DCR Director to investigate and address potential violations to ensure equal protection and fair treatment for all people in New Jersey.

To find out more information or to file a complaint, visit www.njcivilrights.gov.

title: ICE body camera releases must be in agency's 'best interests': Policy - The Hill
description:

Neither encounter was recorded on an officer body camera.
White House border czar Tom Homan said last month that body cameras would provide more transparency around confrontations involving immigration officers.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will equip its officers with body cameras over the next two months, according to reports, but the agency’s policy gives officials broad discretion over footage released to the public that’s deemed in its “best interests.”

More than half of the agency’s field officers have already been outfitted with the body cams, according to The Associated Press. The others are expected to receive them by the end of September.

The rollout follows increased pressure and public scrutiny on the agency after fatal shootings involving ICE officers amid President Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration, leading lawmakers to call on the agency for more transparency.

Under an ICE directive issued in February 2025, officers are required to activate their cameras at the beginning of enforcement activities, including arrests, stops and searches.

If the footage captures an incident involving serious bodily injury or death while in custody, the agency said it will review the video and release it to the public — but only if the administration determines doing so would be “in the best interests of the agency.”

While the agency generally aims to complete that process within 72 hours, the director can withhold or indefinitely delay footage release if there are “specific and compelling circumstances” against releasing it that cannot be solved through redactions.

A review group consisting of senior ICE officials, lawyers and other agency personnel will look through the recordings of serious incidents and issue recommendations to leadership about whether a public release is warranted.

The policy also requires ICE to redact officers’ faces and other identifying information before releasing it.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot a 25-year-old motorist in Maine, and in a separate incident another officer shot and killed a homebuilder driving to work in Houston. Neither encounter was recorded on an officer body camera.

White House border czar Tom Homan said last month that body cameras would provide more transparency around confrontations involving immigration officers.

“I think body cameras are the way to go,” he told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan at the time. “I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action.”

A supporter of President Donald Trump said he is disappointed in the current administration after claiming his fiancée was taken by a group of ICE agents without explanation.

John Gannon, a Republican and Texas businessman, told CBS News that his fiancée, Yasmin Suarez Reyes, 45, was arrested by eight U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at the international airport in Houston last month. The ICE agents allegedly “swarmed” her and “rustled her off into a car” with “no explanation,” Gannon, 75, said.

“You never think, or I never thought a guy like me would ever be involved in something like this,” Gannon said in an interview with the outlet published on Thursday, Aug. 6.

The couple was planning to board a flight to Las Vegas at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport when plainclothes officers took Suarez Reyes, who was born in Venezuela and holds citizenship in Spain, Gannon said.

“I was just in total disbelief,” he told CBS News.

Gannon, who owns more than 1,000 billboards in the U.S. and multiple establishments in Mexico, including a hotel and a restaurant, said he and his fiancée were on their way to a furniture convention when she was detained.

“Nothing like this has ever happened to me,” he continued. “I have several businesses. I’m a law-abiding citizen, and I pay a lot of tax.”

Gannon made it clear that he wasn’t criticizing the Trump administration based on his own political affiliations, as he voted for him in the most recent election.

“I voted for Trump,” he said, adding, “They are picking up law-abiding citizens. They’re destroying families, jobs.”

He added that he would not vote for Trump again, “not after this fiasco,” adding, “This is like the Gestapo.”

In a statement to PEOPLE, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed Suarez Reyes was arrested on July 24.

“On October 24, 2023, she lawfully entered the U.S. and illegally overstayed her lawful admission, which expired on January 19, 2024,” the statement read. “Pending applications do NOT confer legal status. All of her claims will be heard by a Justice Department immigration judge, and she will receive full due process. This Administration is not going to ignore the rule of law.”

PEOPLE reached out to Suarez Reyes’ immigration attorney for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

“For almost two weeks now, she has been in a physical jail cell, when she has done nothing more than follow the laws of the United States and do what our immigration laws allow her to do,” her attorney told CBS News.

“Seriously, it reminds me of a Gestapo system,” Gannon told CBS News. “I would never have thought the United States would act this way.”

text:
The Glenwood Springs City Council voted 6-1 Thursday to pursue legal action against the owner of the Midland Avenue property housing a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility, seeking to stop the building from being used to temporarily hold or detain people.

The council directed City Attorney Karl Hanlon to prepare legal enforcement action, sanctions and injunctive relief against JG Housing Solutions LLC, the owner of the property at 100 Midland Ave., including units 110 and 210, for alleged zoning and land use code violations. The city plans to initially pursue the case in state court rather than directly suing ICE or the U.S. General Services Administration.

JG Housing Solutions LLC did not respond to a request for comment from the Post Independent.

Councilor Ray Schmahl was the only council member to vote against the motion.

The decision comes after the city confirmed ICE continued using the property as a temporary hold facility after the Glenwood Springs Planning and Zoning Commission revoked its special use permit earlier this year.

Emergency medical personnel responded to the facility July 24 for a medical call, and information from that response confirmed people were being held there, Hanlon said.

“That, in my mind, gave me the factual basis to say that it is a ripe claim to potentially bring back to you for action on the zoning violation,” Hanlon said.

Hanlon said the July 24 response gave the city evidence it could use in court to show the property was still being used in a way no longer permitted under city zoning.

The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-1 on April 28 to revoke a special use permit issued in 2003 that allowed ICE to operate a temporary hold facility at the property.

The permit limited holds to 12 hours. The commission revoked it after reviewing evidence showing people had been held beyond that limit on multiple occasions.

Neither ICE, the property owner nor the General Services Administration appealed the decision, which became final around June 4. Under the city’s current zoning code, a temporary hold or detention facility is not a permitted use at the property.

The topic drew a large crowd Thursday, filling the City Council chambers and a second room inside Town Hall used for overflow seating. Many of those in attendance urged the council to enforce the Planning and Zoning Commission’s decision and take action against the property owner.

The revocation does not prevent ICE from continuing to use the property for other purposes allowed under the zoning code, including office or staging space.

Instead, the city would seek preliminary and permanent injunctions preventing the property owner from allowing the site to be used to hold or detain people.

Hanlon recommended going after the property owner rather than directly naming ICE or the General Services Administration because he said that gives the city its best chance of keeping the case in state court.

Even there, he warned the city faces a difficult legal fight.

Asked to estimate the city’s chances of obtaining an injunction, Hanlon said they were probably less than 25%.

The main issue would likely be the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution. The property owner could argue that local zoning enforcement interferes with a core function of the federal government.

Hanlon said the city would argue that prohibiting ICE from holding people at the Glenwood Springs location would not stop the agency from enforcing immigration law.

“If I were the federal government, I would argue that it is immigration enforcement writ large that is the core function that we are impeding,” Hanlon said. “I think my position would be you don’t use the facility that much. You have lots of other opportunities, and nobody is saying you can’t enforce. We’re saying you can’t violate our zoning code by holding people there.”

The potential cost of the case also became a major part of the council’s discussion.

Hanlon estimated the city could spend about $50,000 to reach a preliminary injunction hearing or get through an initial motion to dismiss in state court. A state court case taken through trial could cost between $250,000 and $300,000 and take 18 to 24 months.

A federal case could cost about $100,000 in its early stages and roughly $500,000 through trial, with a trial potentially three years away.

If the city does not obtain a preliminary injunction, the property could continue being used as a hold facility while the case moves forward.

Hanlon also said opposing attorneys could seek sanctions under Rule 11 if they argue the city’s lawsuit is frivolous or groundless. Another law firm has reviewed the issue, and Hanlon said the city believes it has a good-faith basis to bring the case.

Council members generally agreed the city should enforce its land use code but raised concerns about how much money and time should be spent on the case.

Schmahl, who voted against the motion, focused on the financial risk.

“I find my definition of courageous local leadership to be not wasting the taxpayers’ money,” Schmahl said. “I’ve been told over and over again that this is a waste of money.”

Councilor David Townsley also raised concerns about the cost of a long legal battle but said the city should not set a precedent of ignoring violations of its land use code.

Mayor Pro Tem Erin Zalinski said the city had heard months of frustration from residents who believed officials were not acting quickly enough, but said the city needed evidence it could defend in court before taking action.

“We had to wait until we had something that was tangible and actionable and defensible,” Zalinski said.

Public commenters overwhelmingly urged the city to move forward with enforcement. Several specifically encouraged the council to pursue the private property owner in state court rather than directly suing federal agencies.

Glenwood Springs resident Ashley Stahl made that argument during public comment.

“Don’t take this to federal court,” Stahl said. “Don’t name GSA and ICE. The violation in front of you is simple. A private landlord is leasing space for a use our code simply does not permit.”

Hanlon said the city could also pursue a separate municipal court case over the July 24 violation, where city code allows fines of up to $1,000 per day. However, proving continuing daily violations would require the city to show when people were actually being held inside the facility.

He said seeking an injunction in state court offers a more direct path toward stopping the use altogether.

The motion passed 6-1, with Schmahl voting in opposition.

text:
The decision represents another significant development in the growing body of TPS litigation following the Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision limiting judicial review of TPS termination determinations.

Background

South Sudan’s TPS designation was originally terminated by DHS in November 2025, with the designation scheduled to end on January 5, 2026. In February 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts postponed implementation of the termination, finding that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on claims that DHS had violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

That postponement remained in place until the Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision in Mullin v. Doe, which involved TPS terminations for other countries. Following the Supreme Court ruling, the First Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the district court’s postponement order and returned the case to the lower court for additional proceedings.

Court Rejects New Challenges

After the case returned to district court, plaintiffs attempted to advance two new legal theories:

That former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem lacked authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation because that authority belonged exclusively to the Attorney General; and

That DHS violated procedural due process requirements when terminating the designation.

Judge Patti B. Saris rejected both arguments.

Motion to Amend and Renewed Request for Relief Denied

Because the court concluded that both new claims were unlikely to succeed, Judge Saris denied:

Plaintiffs’ request to amend their complaint; and

Plaintiffs’ renewed request to postpone implementation of the TPS termination.

The court held that the proposed new claims would be futile and therefore did not justify further relief.

Erickson Insights and Analysis

The South Sudan ruling is another indication that federal courts are applying the Supreme Court’s Mullin v. Doe precedent broadly when reviewing challenges to TPS terminations. Similar litigation involving other TPS-designated countries remains ongoing, but the August 7 decision suggests that courts may be increasingly reluctant to block DHS termination determinations.

text:
While Donald Trump is highly erratic, you can always rely on him pandering to his MAGA base on immigration-related issues. So it’s no surprise that the defeat in the U.S. Supreme Court of his bid to end birthright citizenship didn’t deter him from coming right back to the well on the subject. On Thursday he signed two new executive orders purporting to address abuses in the current immigration system. While his 2025 EO flatly repudiating the automatic right to citizenship of those born in the United States was struck down by the Supreme Court in the Trump v. Barbara decision on June 30, the new orders appear to nibble around the edges of the issue, as the Associated Press explains:

[The first order] was narrower in scope than the previous one shot down by the Supreme Court and appeared to focus on restricting automatic citizenship to specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations as well as anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States.

It also aimed to restrict birthright citizenship to anyone whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship.”

A second order seeks to curb what Trump called “birth tourism” by increasing restrictions on visitors to the U.S. who want to obtain visas to give birth while in the country.

The number of people ostensibly affected by these orders is pretty limited, notes the Washington Post:

The new orders were certain to face legal challenges, and if they survive, would affect far fewer people than the original. An estimated 15 million undocumented immigrants live in the U.S., while only a few thousand people are foreign lobbyists registered with the Justice Department.

No significant populations of U.S. residents are designated as alien enemies or foreign terrorists, making that provision largely symbolic. The administration faces ongoing litigation over whether it can deport alleged gang members by treating them as alien enemies. …

There is no official data on “birth tourism.” In 2024, fewer than 10,000 babies were born in the U.S. to people with foreign addresses, out of 3.6 million total live births, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention analyzed by the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute.

When Trump announced the new orders Stephen Miller was on hand to offer some demagogic thoughts about “birth tourism,” a concept that fits in well with the presidential aide’s notorious subscription to conspiracy theories about immigrant efforts to rob American blind while rigging elections, as the BBC reported:

“The idea (is) that people come here pretending to be a tourist, pretending to be a visitor,” Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said while standing beside the president on Thursday.

“But the real reason they’re here is to have a child, to make that child an automatic citizen, (to) leave our country and then have a US citizen child,” he said, adding that those children then gain access to welfare benefits, the voting booth, and “all the other rights and privileges that belong solely to Americans”.

While it’s unlikely these orders will ever be successfully enforced, they serve as a pre-midterms reminder to MAGA voters that the administration hasn’t given up on radically restricting legal immigration even as it carries out the mass deportation of undocumented immigrants. It’s as close to the core of Trump’s message and agenda as his related claims that Democrats are regularly stealing elections by deploying the many millions of swarthy illegal voters they’ve lured across the borders by promises of welfare payments and encouragement to commit crimes. Mere Supreme Court decisions won’t stop Trump and Miller from hammering away at this lurid and divisive theme.

text:
A Colorado mountain town is wielding its zoning codes in an attempt to stop federal immigration agents from locking people up in a strip-mall holding cell.

The City Council in Glenwood Springs, the Roaring Fork Valley destination known for its historic hot springs, voted Thursday night to sue the landlord who leases the property used as a processing facility by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after months of pressure from the local community.

The 6-1 vote was met by celebration inside the packed council chambers after dozens spoke out, imploring the council to move forward with the lawsuit.

“For months, we have had rooms like this full of passionate people who plead with us to take action, and it feels like we’re just sitting on our butts doing nothing,” Mayor Pro Tem Erin Zalinski said after voting in favor of the legal action. “We had to wait until we had something tangible and actionable and defensible, so it felt like we weren’t listening and weren’t taking action and we were dying up here… Just know our intentions are to represent our community with integrity and in the best way possible with the tools we have available to us, so what felt like negligence was just trying to be purposeful.”

Wedged between a chiropractor’s office and a gym at 100 Midland Ave., the ICE processing center is used by federal agents to hold immigrants before they are sent to the state’s only large-scale detention facility in Aurora.

For many in the community, the ICE operation was under the radar until the Trump administration’s deportation push prompted people to start asking questions about what was going on inside the building.

After hearing from people detained in the holding facility, filing open records requests with the city and teaching themselves the intricacies of zoning codes, locals like attorney Claire Noone began uncovering information about ICE’s operations in Glenwood Springs and sharing it with residents who demanded accountability from their elected officials.

The inconspicuous facility had been operating for more than 20 years, Noone said she learned at the beginning of the year. In a decades-old agreement, the city granted use of the facility as a detention center, but agents could not hold immigrants for more than 12 hours.

Community members listened to detainees’ accounts of being held longer than that, and found federal records to back that up, which they presented to the city’s planning and zoning commission. The commission went against staff recommendations and voted 5-1 in April to revoke a special-use permit that enabled ICE to detain immigrants at that address.

An unidentified representative from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security denied that immigrants were being held at the Glenwood Springs facility for more than 12 hours. The agency said immigrants held at the strip-mall location are “quickly processed and transferred to permanent housing at a detention facility.”

Legal avenue opens up

The revocation of the special-use permit stripped the facility of its ability to hold immigrants. Neither the U.S. General Services Administration, ICE nor the property owner appealed the city’s revocation within the allotted time limit, Glenwood Springs City Attorney Karl Hanlon said.

The city determined ICE violated the special-use permit revocation on July 24 when the Glenwood Springs Fire Department responded to a call at the location, alerting city officials that the building was still being used to detain immigrants, “making the question of whether to pursue judicial enforcement ripe for consideration,” Hanlon said in a Monday memo to the City Council.

Hanlon advised the elected body to pursue legal avenues as a means of enforcement.

During Thursday’s City Council meeting, Hanlon recommended the council sue the property owner, Jeff Gillespie, in state court over the zoning violation rather than immediately targeting the federal government.

Gillespie operates JG Housing Solutions LLC, which owns the property. Gillespie could not immediately be reached for comment.

The lawsuit does not hinge on the question of whether ICE should be operating at the Glenwood Springs strip mall, Hanlon reminded the council, asking the members to take their feelings about the federal agency out of the equation. Instead, the legal maneuver focuses on whether the City Council can enforce the existing zoning code violation.

Hanlon said the city had a higher likelihood of success suing the landlord in state court, although he admitted it’s still a long shot.

“We’re in uncharted territory here,” Hanlon said during the council meeting. “As an attorney, intellectually, this is an interesting area to practice in. But I have to recognize the law is not necessarily on our side.”

Hanlon predicted ICE would claim the zoning permit revocation interfered with a core function of the federal government, trumping state laws.

Hanlon said he would argue Glenwood Springs isn’t saying ICE can’t enforce the administration’s immigration laws. The city is simply saying ICE can’t violate the zoning regulations by detaining people at the strip-mall facility.

“I would like to be the person who tells you I’m going to get you everything you ever dreamed of,” Hanlon said. “But these are tough cases.”

‘The building was never a secret’

Thursday’s vote is the culmination of months of pressure from the Glenwood Springs community.

In November, Noone got a call from a single mother who was detained at 100 Midland Ave., separated from her young children and in need of language translation. Noone arrived to translate with her 2-year-old on her hip and couldn’t imagine being separated from her baby like the woman in the facility. The lawyer wasn’t allowed inside the building and became curious about what the government was doing.

After months of questions and records requests, Noone discovered that ICE was never granted a final certificate of occupancy allowing the agency to operate in the Glenwood Springs facility — an error from the early 2000s that the city described in a March news release as an “administrative oversight.”

After inspecting the building this year, Glenwood Springs granted the building a certificate of occupancy, but immigrants were still no longer permitted to be held for more than 12 hours. The city confirmed that federal documents showed the facility detained immigrants for longer than 12 hours multiple times.

Community members continued to show up to city meetings demanding their leaders stand up to ICE and hold the federal agency accountable for its violation of the city’s zoning code.

Glenwood Springs residents said during Thursday’s meeting that they had been waved off by the city for months until proof the community gathered about the building’s purpose and violations was undeniable.

“This building was never a secret,” said Ashley Stahl. “Our immigrant neighbors have known exactly what happened at this building for years. They were right first and nobody listened. What took us 20 years wasn’t finding out what was happening, it was listening.”

Hanlon, the city attorney, said Glenwood Springs was gearing up for a tough legal fight that would likely take years and, potentially, cost hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees.

“If little old Glenwood Springs can do this, anybody can,” Stahl said.

A Maine Medical Center nurse who was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at a Boston airport is out of custody and on her way home to Maine one day after her colleagues held a protest demanding her release.

U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, and the Maine State Nurses Association announced the release of Debora Kapisha, a registered nurse at the hospital, on Thursday.

Kapisha was detained by ICE last week while traveling through Boston Logan International Airport, according to the nurses union. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Wednesday that Kapisha was apprehended July 30 for allegedly overstaying a visa that expired in November 2024.

Nurses protested outside Maine Medical Center in Portland on Wednesday to bring awareness to their colleague’s detention and advocate for her release.

“We knew we had to take action, first to stop her from being transferred out of New England while in custody, but also to demand her release,” Kelli Brennan, a registered nurse at Maine Med and nurse leader with the union, said in a statement Thursday following Kapisha’s release.

At the protest, Kapisha’s co-workers described her as a kind and compassionate woman who worked hard to earn a nursing degree. More than 100 people, including nurses and community advocates, gathered to call for her release.

Kapisha, who is from Zambia in southern Africa, is an asylum seeker who is legally authorized to work in the country, the nurses union says.

The union plans to hold a news conference about Kapisha’s release along Portland’s Western Promenade, near Maine Medical Center, at 11:30 a.m. Friday.

Pingree noted in her announcement of Kapisha’s release that it can take years for asylum cases to run their course.

“Debora followed the law to apply for asylum the legal way,” Pingree said in a social media post. “Just because our immigration system is broken doesn’t mean we should punish innocent people — especially those working on the front lines of our health care system.”

MaineHealth said that it provided support to Kapisha’s attorneys and contacted Maine’s congressional delegation to request assistance with her case.

“We are grateful to Maine’s congressional delegation and to all of those who worked to ensure that our care team member could return to her family and to her colleagues at MaineHealth Maine Medical Center Portland,” hospital Chief Operating Officer Matt Wolden said in a news release Thursday. “We take care to ensure that everyone who works for us is legally authorized to do so and are glad that immigration authorities were able to clear up this case quickly.”

Puneet Maharaj, executive director of National Nurses United, said in a written statement that Kapisha’s release “is a testament to the power of organized nurses.”

“Nurses in Maine found out one of their own was locked up and sprung into action to get her out,” Maharaj said.

text:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. Those ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

A second executive order targets so-called birth tourism, in which pregnant women travel to the United States on tourist visas to give birth so their children will obtain U.S. citizenship. White House officials acknowledged the practice is relatively uncommon but said the administration wants to prevent people from using tourist visas for that purpose.

Officials did not explain how they would determine whether a traveler intends to give birth in the United States. Reporters asked how immigration officials would decide whether someone is too far along in a pregnancy to enter on a tourist visa, but the administration did not provide details.

Instead, officials pointed to a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act that allows the president to prescribe certain limitations and exceptions under existing immigration law.

The orders appear to be the administration's latest effort to limit birthright citizenship following a recent Supreme Court decision reaffirming that most people born in the United States are automatically U.S. citizens.
